tabs.title: Ostomy Flow Sheet — POD 1, Sigmoid Colostomy

questions.stem: A 63-year-old client had a sigmoid colostomy created yesterday for colon cancer. The nurse reviews the ostomy flow sheet in the exhibit at 1600. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Cut the pouch opening larger to relieve pressure on the stoma
Document the dusky, dry stoma findings on the flow sheet
Notify the surgeon of the change in stoma color and surface
Reassess the stoma in 1 hour to confirm the color trend
optionRationales: Incorrect. A pouch opening that is too tight can harm a swollen stoma, but resizing it does not restore blood flow, and the trend shows a perfusion problem that needs the surgeon now.
Incorrect. Documentation is required, but recording the finding does not get the stoma evaluated; the surgeon must be notified first.
Correct. A stoma that changes from beefy red and moist to dusky purple and dry is losing its blood supply, and the tissue can die without prompt surgical evaluation.
Incorrect. Rechecking is reasonable when one finding is unclear, but three entries already show a worsening trend, and waiting delays care for tissue that may be dying.
questions.rationale: A healthy stoma is moist and pink to beefy red because it has a rich blood supply. The flow sheet shows a trend from beefy red to dark red to dusky purple with a dry, dull surface, which means perfusion is getting worse. A pale, dusky, purple, or black stoma must be reported to the surgeon immediately because the tissue can die. Resizing the pouch, documenting, or rechecking later are all reasonable nursing actions, but none of them gets the stoma evaluated, and the trend is already clear.
questions.takeaway: A stoma that turns dusky, purple, or black is a perfusion emergency; report it to the surgeon immediately.
questions.hintContent: Compare the 1600 findings with what a healthy stoma should look like, and think about what stoma color reflects.
questions.hintStrategy: When an exhibit shows a trend over time, ask whether it is getting better or worse; a worsening perfusion trend calls for prompt notification.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client on day 3 after creation of an ileostomy for ulcerative colitis. Which assessment finding requires the nurse's priority follow-up?
options: Heart rate of 118/min and dizziness when standing
Red, irritated skin where the pouch barrier sits
Small spot of bleeding when the stoma is cleaned
Client turns away and will not look at the stoma
optionRationales: Correct. Ileostomy output is liquid and frequent, so the client is at high risk for fluid and electrolyte loss; a fast heart rate and dizziness on standing suggest dehydration, a circulation problem that comes first.
Incorrect. Irritated peristomal skin needs follow-up because ileostomy stool is enzyme-rich, but it is a local skin problem and ranks below signs of low fluid volume.
Incorrect. Reporting bleeding from a stoma is a reasonable instinct, but a stoma has a rich blood supply and a small spot of bleeding when it is cleaned is expected.
Incorrect. Refusing to look at the stoma is a body-image concern that needs support, but psychosocial needs come after a physiologic problem.
questions.rationale: An ileostomy drains stool from the small intestine before the colon can absorb water, so the output is liquid, frequent, and enzyme-rich. That makes dehydration and electrolyte loss the major physiologic risk, which is why intake and output are monitored closely. Tachycardia and dizziness on standing are cues that fluid volume is low and need follow-up now. Irritated skin and body-image distress also need attention, but they rank below a circulation problem, and slight bleeding when a stoma is cleaned is expected.
questions.takeaway: With an ileostomy, liquid output is expected, but signs of fluid volume loss such as tachycardia and orthostatic dizziness need priority follow-up.
questions.hintContent: Sort each finding into expected or unexpected for a stoma from the small intestine, then think about what liquid output does to fluid balance.
questions.hintStrategy: In a "priority follow-up" item, cross off every finding that is expected for the condition; the one left is usually a sign of a physiologic complication.

questions.stem: A client returned to the unit 30 minutes ago after an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with throat numbing and sedation. The client is awake and says, "My throat is so dry. Can I please have some water?" Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Review the provider's post-procedure diet order
Offer ice chips to soothe the throat
Raise the head of the bed before giving fluids
Check that the gag reflex has returned
optionRationales: Incorrect. Following the diet order is appropriate, but the order does not show whether this client can swallow safely right now; only a gag reflex check does.
Incorrect. Ice chips seem harmless, but they melt into water and carry the same aspiration risk as fluids.
Incorrect. Raising the head of the bed lowers aspiration risk, but it does not make oral intake safe if the gag reflex has not returned.
Correct. The throat was numbed for the scope, so the nurse must confirm the gag reflex has returned before giving anything by mouth to prevent aspiration.
questions.rationale: During an EGD the throat is numbed so the scope can pass through the mouth into the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. Until that numbing wears off, the client may not protect the airway when swallowing. The nurse gives nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns, which prevents aspiration. Ice chips seem harmless, which makes them tempting, but they turn into water in the mouth and pose the same risk.
questions.takeaway: After an EGD, nothing by mouth, including ice chips, until the gag reflex returns.
questions.hintContent: Think about what was done to the throat to allow the scope to pass, and what that means for swallowing.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client asks for something after a procedure, look for the option that confirms safety (assessment) before the option that meets the request.

questions.stem: An endoscopy recovery nurse receives updates on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client 1 day after a barium enema who reports chalky white stool this morning and asks if it is normal
A client 2 hours after colonoscopy and polyp removal who has a rigid abdomen and fever
A client 1 hour after EGD whose gag reflex has not yet returned and who is NPO
A client drinking a colonoscopy preparation who has frequent yellow liquid stools
optionRationales: Incorrect. White or chalky stool for a day or two after barium is expected.
Correct. A rigid abdomen and fever after colonoscopy with polyp removal suggest bowel perforation, a surgical emergency.
Incorrect. A delayed gag reflex is expected early after EGD, and NPO status is already keeping this client safe.
Incorrect. Frequent yellow liquid stools show the preparation is working as intended; the goal is clear liquid output.
questions.rationale: Prioritization means finding the client whose findings point to an unstable or life-threatening problem. After colonoscopy, especially when tissue is removed, severe pain, distension, fever, or a rigid abdomen point to perforation and must be reported immediately. White stool after barium, a slow-to-return gag reflex in an NPO client, and liquid stool during bowel prep are all expected. The EGD client may look tempting because airway safety matters, but the client is already protected by staying NPO.
questions.takeaway: After colonoscopy, a rigid abdomen, fever, or severe pain signals possible perforation and outranks expected procedure effects.
questions.hintContent: For each client, ask whether the finding is an expected effect of the procedure or a sign of a complication.
questions.hintStrategy: In a four-client prioritization item, eliminate the expected findings first; the client with an unexpected, dangerous finding goes first.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old client who takes ferrous sulfate daily reports two black, tarry stools since this morning. The client feels lightheaded. Vital signs are heart rate 108/min and blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg; yesterday they were 82/min and 132/78 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Reassure the client that iron commonly turns stool black
Report the findings promptly as possible GI bleeding
Hold the next iron dose and recheck the stool tomorrow
Send a stool sample for occult blood testing and wait for the results
optionRationales: Incorrect. Iron can darken stool, but it does not cause tachycardia, hypotension, and lightheadedness.
Correct. Black, tarry stool with a rising heart rate, falling blood pressure, and lightheadedness suggests upper GI bleeding and needs prompt provider notification.
Incorrect. Waiting until tomorrow delays care for a client who may be bleeding now.
Incorrect. Testing may be ordered, but the vital sign changes mean the nurse should not wait for a result before reporting.
questions.rationale: Black, tarry stool (melena) usually means bleeding high in the GI tract, although iron supplements can also turn stool black. The nurse should never assume the cause is the iron, especially when other cues are present. Here the heart rate has risen and the blood pressure has dropped since yesterday, and the client feels lightheaded, which together suggest blood loss. The tempting answer is to reassure the client about iron, but that ignores the change in vital signs.
questions.takeaway: Black stool in a client on iron still needs investigation, and with tachycardia or hypotension it must be reported promptly as possible GI bleeding.
questions.hintContent: Look beyond the stool color: what do the changes in heart rate and blood pressure add?
questions.hintStrategy: When an option offers a harmless explanation, check whether all of the cues fit it; if some do not, choose the action that addresses the dangerous possibility.

questions.stem: The nurse is assisting a provider with a digital rectal exam on a client with suspected fecal impaction. During the exam, the client says, "I feel faint," and the heart rate on the monitor drops from 78/min to 46/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the provider to stop the exam, then assess the client
Check the client's blood pressure and level of consciousness
Encourage the client to take slow, deep breaths
Prepare atropine in case the heart rate keeps dropping
optionRationales: Correct. Stimulating the rectum can trigger a vagal response that slows the heart rate, so the stimulation must stop first, and then the client is assessed.
Incorrect. These assessments are needed, but checking them while the exam continues lets the vagal stimulus keep slowing the heart; stop the cause first.
Incorrect. Slow breathing may calm the client, but it does not remove the vagal stimulus that is slowing the heart.
Incorrect. Atropine may be needed if bradycardia persists, but stopping the stimulation often resolves it and must come first.
questions.rationale: Rectal stimulation during a digital rectal exam or removal of impacted stool can stimulate the vagus nerve. Vagal stimulation slows the heart rate and can cause dizziness or fainting. The first step is to remove the cause by stopping the exam, then assess the pulse, blood pressure, and level of consciousness. Checking vital signs or preparing atropine is tempting because the heart rate is low, but those steps come after the stimulus that is causing the problem has been stopped.
questions.takeaway: Bradycardia and faintness during rectal stimulation signal a vagal response; stop the stimulation first.
questions.hintContent: Think about which nerve is stimulated during a rectal exam and what it does to the heart.
questions.hintStrategy: When a procedure causes an adverse response, the first action is usually to stop the procedure that triggered it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client is being discharged after an outpatient barium enema. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to include in the discharge teaching?
options: Drink extra fluids and take the prescribed laxative
Stay on clear liquids for the next 24 hours
Report any white or light-colored stools
Avoid eating or drinking until your gag reflex has returned
optionRationales: Correct. Barium can harden in the colon and cause constipation or impaction, so fluids and the prescribed laxative help the client pass it.
Incorrect. Clear liquids are part of the preparation before bowel tests, not the priority after a barium enema.
Incorrect. White or chalky stool for a day or two after barium is expected and does not need to be reported.
Incorrect. The gag reflex matters after an EGD, where the throat is numbed, not after a barium enema.
questions.rationale: In a barium enema, contrast is placed into the colon through the rectum so x-rays can outline the bowel. If barium stays in the colon, it can harden and cause constipation or even impaction. The key aftercare is fluids and a laxative as ordered, and the client should report not passing the barium. Clients often worry about white stool, and a half-prepared student may choose to report it, but white or chalky stool is the expected sign that barium is leaving the body.
questions.takeaway: After barium, push fluids and give the ordered laxative; white stool for a day or two is expected.
questions.hintContent: Consider what barium can do if it stays in the colon.
questions.hintStrategy: For discharge teaching after a procedure, choose the instruction that prevents the most likely complication of that specific procedure.

tabs.title: I&O and Vital Signs — New Ileostomy, POD 4

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with a new ileostomy reports feeling "washed out" and does not want to drink because "more just comes out." The nurse reviews the data in the exhibit. Which concern is the priority?
options: Impaired peristomal skin from contact with enzyme-rich stool
Disturbed body image related to the new stoma
Fluid volume deficit from high ileostomy output
Risk for infection at the surgical incision
optionRationales: Incorrect. Skin protection matters with ileostomy output, but nothing in the data shows skin breakdown, and a physiologic fluid loss comes first.
Incorrect. The client may be struggling emotionally, but psychosocial concerns come after an active physiologic problem.
Correct. Output rose to 1,900 mL while intake and urine output fell and the heart rate rose, all cues of a developing fluid volume deficit.
Incorrect. No cues of infection, such as fever or incisional redness, are provided.
questions.rationale: Ileostomy output is liquid and frequent, so these clients are at high risk for dehydration and electrolyte loss. The exhibit shows output increasing while oral intake drops, urine output falls below expected, the heart rate climbs, and the membranes become dry. Together these cues point to fluid volume deficit, which needs to be reported and treated. Skin damage is a real ileostomy concern and is tempting, but it is only a risk here, while fluid loss is already happening.
questions.takeaway: High ileostomy output with falling intake and urine output is a fluid volume emergency in the making; it outranks skin and body-image concerns.
questions.hintContent: Compare day 3 with day 4 for intake, output, heart rate, and membranes, and decide which body system the changes point to.
questions.hintStrategy: When several problems are possible, choose the one that is actually supported by the data and is physiologic before one that is only a risk or psychosocial.

questions.stem: During a bowel assessment, the nurse notes that a 49-year-old client's stool is clay-colored. The client has had no recent imaging with contrast and takes no supplements. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: Bleeding may be occurring high in the GI tract
Bleeding may be occurring near the anus
Stool is moving too quickly through the colon
Bile may not be reaching the intestine
optionRationales: Incorrect. Bleeding high in the GI tract produces black, tarry stool (melena), not pale stool.
Incorrect. Bleeding low in the GI tract or near the anus produces red blood in or on the stool.
Incorrect. Fast transit causes liquid stool, but it does not remove the brown color.
Correct. Clay-colored or white stool means bile is not reaching the bowel, since bile gives stool its brown color.
questions.rationale: Stool color gives clues about what is happening in the GI tract. Clay-colored or white stool means bile is not reaching the bowel, and it can also be seen for a day or two after barium, which this client has not had. Black, tarry stool suggests bleeding high in the tract, and red stool suggests bleeding low in the tract or near the anus. Students often link any abnormal color to bleeding, but pale stool is the one change that points to bile rather than blood.
questions.takeaway: Clay-colored stool means bile is not reaching the bowel, unless the client recently had barium.
questions.hintContent: Recall which substance normally gives stool its brown color.
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem rules out a common harmless cause (like recent barium), it is pointing you toward the pathologic explanation.

questions.stem: A client who had abdominal surgery 2 days ago has a slightly distended abdomen. After inspecting the abdomen, the nurse listens in the right lower quadrant for 30 seconds and hears no bowel sounds. What should the nurse do next?
options: Document that bowel sounds are absent in all four quadrants
Palpate the abdomen deeply to stimulate bowel sounds
Continue listening for several minutes in each quadrant
Percuss the right lower quadrant to locate any stool
optionRationales: Incorrect. Thirty seconds in one quadrant is not enough to call bowel sounds absent anywhere.
Incorrect. Palpation can alter peristalsis, which gives a false picture of bowel activity, so it comes after auscultation.
Correct. Before documenting bowel sounds as absent, the nurse listens for several minutes, in all four quadrants.
Incorrect. Percussion comes after a complete auscultation, and it does not tell the nurse whether bowel sounds are present.
questions.rationale: For the abdomen, the order is inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation, because pressing on the belly can change peristalsis. Normal bowel sounds are irregular, so short silences are common. To call bowel sounds absent, the nurse must listen for several minutes, and in each of the four quadrants. Documenting absent sounds is the tempting choice because the client just had surgery, but documenting after 30 seconds in one spot would be an inaccurate assessment.
questions.takeaway: Listen in all four quadrants for several minutes before documenting absent bowel sounds, and auscultate before you palpate.
questions.hintContent: Think about how long and in how many places the nurse must listen before deciding sounds are absent.
questions.hintStrategy: When an option documents a conclusion, check whether the assessment behind it is complete; finish the assessment first.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a stable 66-year-old client with a colostomy created 3 years ago who was admitted for pneumonia. Which task is appropriate for the nurse to delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
options: Inspecting the stoma for changes in color
Emptying the pouch and measuring the output
Teaching the client which foods cause gas
Evaluating the peristomal skin for breakdown
optionRationales: Incorrect. Inspecting the stoma for perfusion changes is assessment, which the nurse keeps.
Correct. Emptying an established ostomy pouch and measuring output is a routine task for a stable client that AP can perform and report.
Incorrect. Teaching is a nursing responsibility and cannot be delegated to AP.
Incorrect. Evaluating skin integrity requires nursing assessment and judgment.
questions.rationale: Delegation depends on the task and the stability of the client. This client is stable and the colostomy is well established, so emptying the pouch and measuring output is routine care AP can do, with instructions to report anything unusual. Assessing the stoma, evaluating the skin, and teaching all require nursing judgment and stay with the nurse. Inspecting the stoma may seem like simple observation, but judging whether its color is normal is an assessment.
questions.takeaway: AP can empty and measure an established ostomy pouch for a stable client; stoma assessment, skin evaluation, and teaching stay with the nurse.
questions.hintContent: Separate the tasks into routine care versus tasks that need assessment, teaching, or evaluation.
questions.hintStrategy: For delegation items, eliminate any option containing assess, evaluate, inspect for changes, or teach.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client is scheduled for a colorectal transit study to evaluate long-standing constipation. Which statement by the client shows a need for further teaching?
options: "I'll keep using my nightly senna so I don't get backed up."
"I'll swallow a capsule that has markers inside it."
"I may need several x-rays over a few days to track where the markers are."
"The test shows how fast things move through my bowel."
optionRationales: Correct. This statement needs correcting: laxatives and enemas are usually avoided during the study so the results reflect the bowel's real speed.
Incorrect. This is accurate; the client swallows a capsule containing markers.
Incorrect. This is accurate; x-rays over several days show how the markers move.
Incorrect. This is accurate; the study measures how quickly material moves through the colon.
questions.rationale: A colorectal transit study evaluates constipation and slow motility. The client swallows a capsule of markers, and x-rays taken over several days show how far the markers travel. Laxatives and enemas are usually avoided during the study because they would speed transit and hide the real problem. The client's wish to avoid feeling backed up is understandable, but continuing senna would make the test results meaningless.
questions.takeaway: During a colorectal transit study, the client avoids laxatives and enemas so the results show the bowel's true speed.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the test is trying to measure and what a laxative would do to that measurement.
questions.hintStrategy: In a "needs further teaching" item, look for the statement that would interfere with the purpose of the test.

questions.stem: A nursing student caring for a client with a new ascending colostomy says, "The pouch has liquid stool in it. I think I should report that the output is abnormal." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Measure the output first, then we'll decide if it needs reporting."
"That's expected now, but it should become formed within a week."
"That's expected. Little water is absorbed before the ascending colon."
"Check the barrier seal, because liquid stool can cause leaks."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Measuring output is good practice, but it delays correcting the student's misunderstanding; liquid output from this stoma is expected regardless of the amount.
Incorrect. Output from a new stoma can change as the bowel recovers, but an ascending colostomy stays liquid to semi-liquid because the colon has little chance to absorb water.
Correct. An ascending colostomy is early in the colon, so little water has been absorbed and liquid to semi-liquid output is expected.
Incorrect. Liquid output can loosen a barrier, so checking the seal is useful, but it does not answer whether the output is abnormal.
questions.rationale: The colon absorbs water as stool moves along it. The farther along the bowel the stoma is, the more formed the stool will be. An ascending colostomy is near the start of the colon, so its output is liquid to semi-liquid, much like an ileostomy, while a sigmoid colostomy produces formed stool. The student is assuming that all colostomies produce formed stool, which is the misconception this item targets.
questions.takeaway: Predict ostomy output from location: ileostomy and ascending colostomy are liquid; sigmoid colostomy is formed.
questions.hintContent: Picture where the ascending colon sits along the path of stool and how much water has been removed by that point.
questions.hintStrategy: When a student or colleague worries about a finding, first decide whether it is expected for that client before deciding whether to report it.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: During an admission bowel history, a 67-year-old client says, "I'm fine. I just take a laxative every night." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "How long have you taken it, and what happens if you skip a night?"
"That's fine, as long as you have a bowel movement every day."
"You should stop the laxative starting today so your bowel can recover on its own."
"Which brand do you use, so I can add it to your list?"
optionRationales: Correct. Nightly laxative use is an important finding, and this open question explores how long it has been used and whether the client now depends on it.
Incorrect. A daily bowel movement is not required, and this response accepts routine laxative use without assessing it.
Incorrect. Telling the client to stop before assessing the pattern is premature and is not the nurse's decision alone.
Incorrect. The medication list matters, but this misses the more important cue of possible laxative dependence.
questions.rationale: A bowel history includes the use of elimination aids such as laxatives, enemas, and routines. Daily laxative use can weaken the bowel's natural reflexes and lead to dependence, so the statement is a cue to explore, not a passing comment. Asking how long and what happens without it tells the nurse whether the bowel now relies on the laxative. Advising the client to stop right away is tempting, but the nurse assesses first, and changes are planned with the provider.
questions.takeaway: Treat routine laxative use as an assessment cue: ask how long and what happens without it.
questions.hintContent: Consider what long-term laxative use does to the bowel's natural reflexes.
questions.hintStrategy: In a best-response item during assessment, choose the open question that gathers more data over advice or reassurance.

questions.stem: A client is drinking a bowel preparation the evening before a colonoscopy. At 2100 the client tells the nurse, "I'm still passing brown liquid with some bits of stool in it." How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: The bowel is ready because the stool has become liquid
The preparation has failed, so the colonoscopy should be canceled for today
The prep is not working, so a tap-water enema should be added
The prep is not complete yet and should continue as ordered
optionRationales: Incorrect. Liquid stool shows the prep is working, but liquid is not the goal; the output must be clear so the colon lining can be seen.
Incorrect. A poor prep can lead to rescheduling, but the prep is still in progress, and one evening check does not mean it has failed.
Incorrect. Enemas are sometimes ordered when a prep falls short, but the prep is still working as expected and an enema needs a provider's order.
Correct. The prep continues until the output is clear liquid; brown liquid with particles means the colon is not yet clean.
questions.rationale: Before a colonoscopy, the client follows clear liquids and a laxative prep until the output is clear liquid. A clean colon lets the provider see the lining, take tissue samples, and remove polyps. Brown liquid with bits of stool shows the prep is working but is not finished. The tempting choice is to call the bowel ready because the stool is liquid, but liquid is not the same as clear.
questions.takeaway: Colonoscopy prep is complete when the output is clear liquid, not merely liquid.
questions.hintContent: Recall the end point the bowel prep is aiming for.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, compare the finding with the exact goal of the intervention.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse performs a bowel assessment, including an abdominal exam, on a 45-year-old client admitted with abdominal pain in the left lower quadrant. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Inspect the abdomen for shape, scars, and distension first
Percuss the abdomen before auscultating to stimulate peristalsis
Inspect the anus and rectal area for hemorrhoids or fissures
Palpate the left lower quadrant first to localize the pain
Auscultate all four quadrants before palpating
Palpate lightly before palpating more deeply
optionRationales: Correct. Inspection comes first, noting shape, scars, visible movement, and distension.
Incorrect. Percussion follows auscultation, and the goal is to hear bowel sounds as they are, not to stimulate them.
Correct. The bowel assessment includes inspecting and palpating the rectum and anus for hemorrhoids, fissures, and skin breakdown.
Incorrect. The painful area is palpated last so the client does not tense up and limit the rest of the exam.
Correct. Auscultation comes before palpation because palpation can alter peristalsis.
Correct. Light palpation comes first, followed by deeper palpation, checking for tenderness and masses.
questions.rationale: The abdominal exam order is inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation, which differs from most body systems. Auscultation comes before touching because palpation or percussion can change peristalsis and give a false result. Palpation starts light and moves deeper, with any painful area examined last. The tempting error is to go straight to the painful quadrant, but doing so first causes guarding and makes the rest of the exam unreliable.
questions.takeaway: Abdomen: inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate, with light before deep and the painful area last.
questions.hintContent: Recall why the abdomen is examined in a different order from other body systems.
questions.hintStrategy: For a procedure-sequence SATA, check each option against the correct order and reject any step that is out of place.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old client is scheduled for an outpatient EGD to evaluate upper abdominal pain. Which information should the nurse include when preparing the client? Select all that apply.
options: "Report severe pain or bleeding after the procedure."
"Don't eat or drink anything before the test for as long as you are told."
"Your throat will be numbed so the scope can pass through your mouth."
"You will drink a bowel-cleansing preparation the night before."
"You will need to sign a consent form before the procedure."
"After the test, you can drink as soon as you are fully awake."
optionRationales: Correct. Severe pain or bleeding after an EGD can signal a complication and should be reported.
Correct. The client is NPO before an EGD.
Correct. The throat is numbed to allow the scope to pass into the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum.
Incorrect. A bowel-cleansing prep is used before a colonoscopy, not an EGD.
Correct. An EGD is an invasive procedure that requires informed consent.
Incorrect. The client must wait until the gag reflex returns before drinking, even after waking.
questions.rationale: An EGD uses a scope passed through the mouth to view the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. Before the test, the client is NPO and signs a consent, and the throat is numbed. After the test, nothing is given by mouth until the gag reflex returns, which prevents aspiration, and severe pain or bleeding is reported. A common mix-up is to borrow colonoscopy prep, but the bowel does not need cleansing for a scope that enters through the mouth.
questions.takeaway: EGD: NPO and consent before; nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns after.
questions.hintContent: Picture the route the scope takes, and match each instruction to that route.
questions.hintStrategy: When two procedures are similar, sort each option by which procedure it truly belongs to.

questions.stem: A home health nurse reviews stool observations recorded by the families of several adult clients. Which findings should the nurse follow up on? Select all that apply.
options: Greasy, floating stools with a very foul odor
White, chalky stool the day after a barium enema
Black, tarry stool in a client who takes no iron
Brown, soft, formed stool every other day
Narrow, pencil-shaped stools for the past month
Darker brown stool after eating more red meat
optionRationales: Correct. Greasy, floating stool suggests large amounts of fat, an abnormal constituent.
Incorrect. White or chalky stool for a day or two after barium is expected.
Correct. Black, tarry stool without iron use suggests bleeding high in the GI tract.
Incorrect. Soft, brown, formed stool every other day is within the wide normal range.
Correct. Narrow, pencil-shaped stool can mean something is narrowing the bowel, such as a mass.
Incorrect. Diet affects stool color and odor, and a darker brown stool after a diet change is within normal variation.
questions.rationale: The nurse observes stool color, consistency, shape, amount, odor, and abnormal constituents. Black, tarry stool suggests upper GI bleeding, and narrow, pencil-shaped stool can mean the bowel is being narrowed by a mass. Large amounts of fat (greasy, floating stool), pus, or mucus are abnormal constituents. Normal frequency ranges from several times a day to a few times a week, so stool every other day is not abnormal; diet can shift color and odor, and white stool right after barium is expected.
questions.takeaway: Follow up on black or tarry stool, pencil-thin stool, and greasy fatty stool; white stool right after barium and diet-related color shifts are expected.
questions.hintContent: Check each finding against the six stool characteristics and what is normal for each.
questions.hintStrategy: For SATA findings items, judge each option on its own against normal; do not assume a certain number are correct.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 55-year-old client had a colonoscopy with removal of two polyps and is being discharged home with a family member. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: "Some gas and mild cramping are expected today."
"Expect your stool to be white or chalky for a few days."
"Report a fever after you get home."
"Report heavy bleeding from the rectum."
"Take a laxative tonight to help pass the contrast."
"Call right away for severe abdominal pain or a hard, swollen belly."
optionRationales: Correct. Air is used to open the colon during the scope, so gas and cramping are expected afterward.
Incorrect. White or chalky stool follows a barium enema, not a colonoscopy.
Correct. Fever after colonoscopy can be a sign of perforation.
Correct. Heavy rectal bleeding, especially after polyp removal, must be reported.
Incorrect. Laxatives after testing are used to clear barium; no contrast is used in a colonoscopy.
Correct. Severe pain, distension, or a rigid abdomen can signal perforation, which must be reported immediately.
questions.rationale: After colonoscopy, the client is monitored as sedation wears off, and gas and cramping are expected. Signs of perforation, including severe abdominal pain, distension, fever, or a rigid abdomen, and heavy rectal bleeding must be reported immediately. Taking tissue or removing polyps raises the risk of bleeding and perforation. White stool and a post-test laxative belong to barium enema aftercare, a common mix-up when several bowel tests are learned together.
questions.takeaway: After colonoscopy, expect gas and cramping; report severe pain, a rigid or distended abdomen, fever, or heavy bleeding.
questions.hintContent: Separate the expected effects of having a scope in the colon from the signs of a tear or bleeding.
questions.hintStrategy: When teaching options mention a different procedure's aftercare, eliminate them even if they sound helpful.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a 29-year-old client with a new ileostomy created after a bowel perforation. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Expect output to become formed within a week
Plan to stop using a pouch once output is regular
Fit the skin barrier closely around the stoma
Inspect the peristomal skin with each pouch change
Watch for signs of electrolyte loss
Monitor intake and output closely
optionRationales: Incorrect. Ileostomy output stays liquid to pasty because it never passes through the colon.
Incorrect. Ileostomy output drains often and fairly constantly, so a pouch is always needed.
Correct. Ileostomy output contains digestive enzymes that quickly damage skin, so the barrier must fit closely.
Correct. Leaking enzyme-rich stool damages the skin quickly, so the skin is inspected every time.
Correct. Losing large amounts of liquid stool also means losing electrolytes.
Correct. Liquid, frequent ileostomy output puts the client at high risk for dehydration, so I&O is monitored.
questions.rationale: An ileostomy is made from the ileum, so stool leaves before the colon can absorb water. The output is liquid to pasty, drains often, and contains digestive enzymes that damage skin within a short time. Nursing care focuses on fluid and electrolyte balance (close I&O) and on protecting the peristomal skin with a well-fitted barrier and frequent inspection. Expecting formed, predictable output is tempting, but that describes a sigmoid colostomy, not an ileostomy.
questions.takeaway: Ileostomy care centers on two risks: fluid and electrolyte loss, and skin damage from enzyme-rich output.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the output of a small-intestine stoma is like and what it does to the body and the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: In a care-planning SATA, include interventions that address the main risks of the condition and reject options that describe a different condition.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 50-year-old client how to collect stool at home for a fecal occult blood test as part of colorectal cancer screening. Which client statements show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
options: "I'll scoop the sample out of the toilet water after flushing."
"I'll use a clean container or a collection hat in the toilet."
"I'll follow the diet and medicine instructions on the kit."
"I'll get the sample to the lab promptly after I collect it."
"I'll keep urine and toilet paper out of the sample."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Toilet water contaminates the sample; stool is collected in a container or hat before it reaches the water.
Correct. A clean container or a hat placed in the toilet keeps the sample uncontaminated.
Correct. Some occult blood tests require diet or medication changes before collection.
Correct. Fresh samples should reach the lab promptly.
Correct. Urine and toilet paper can contaminate the sample and affect the result.
questions.rationale: A fecal occult blood test looks for hidden blood in stool and is used to screen for colorectal cancer. The sample must be collected without mixing in urine, toilet paper, or toilet water, using a clean container or a hat placed under the seat. The client follows any diet or medication instructions for the test and sends fresh samples to the lab promptly. Collecting from the toilet water may seem easier, but contamination can make the result unreliable.
questions.takeaway: Collect stool for testing in a clean container or hat, free of urine, paper, and toilet water, and send it promptly.
questions.hintContent: Think about anything that could contaminate the sample or change the result.
questions.hintStrategy: For a teaching-evaluation SATA, choose every statement that protects the accuracy of the test.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 76-year-old client with heart failure has a prescribed fluid restriction of 1,500 mL/day and reports hard stools every 4 to 5 days. The client eats white bread and little produce. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Encourage at least 2,000 mL of fluid daily to soften the stool
Add fiber gradually and spread the allowed fluid across the day
Double the fiber in the diet starting with tomorrow's breakfast
Give a bulk-forming laxative with a small sip of water at bedtime
optionRationales: Incorrect. The usual 2,000 mL goal does not apply when the provider has ordered a fluid restriction for heart failure.
Correct. Fiber is added gradually while the allowed fluid is spaced through the day, which treats constipation without breaking the restriction.
Incorrect. Increasing fiber suddenly causes gas and bloating, and fiber needs fluid to work.
Incorrect. Bulk-forming laxatives must be taken with a full glass of water, or they can harden stool and cause blockage.
questions.rationale: Fluid and fiber are the first-line tools for constipation, and they work together because fiber holds water in the stool. The usual goal is about 2,000 mL or more of fluid per day, but the nurse must check for restrictions first, as in heart failure. Here the best plan is to increase fiber gradually and spread the permitted fluid evenly through the day, and the nurse can collaborate with the provider if constipation continues. The tempting answer applies the standard fluid goal without noticing the restriction, which could worsen heart failure.
questions.takeaway: Always check for a fluid restriction before pushing fluids, and increase fiber gradually.
questions.hintContent: Look for a detail in the stem that changes the usual fluid recommendation.
questions.hintStrategy: When a standard intervention conflicts with a provider order or a coexisting condition, the order and the client's safety win.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

tabs.title: Nursing Note 1000
tabs.html: No bowel movement since admission 3 days ago. Passing flatus. Bowel sounds hypoactive in all quadrants. Abdomen soft, mildly distended, nontender. No nausea or vomiting. Using oxycodone 4–5 times daily.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client reports feeling "full and backed up." The nurse reviews the medication record and note in the exhibit. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Hold oxycodone until the client has a bowel movement
Ask the provider about adding a stimulant laxative
Double the docusate dose for the rest of the day
Encourage extra fluids and high-fiber foods at meals
optionRationales: Incorrect. Opioids do slow the bowel, but withholding pain medication without an order leaves pain untreated and limits the walking that helps the bowel.
Correct. For opioid-induced constipation, a softener alone is usually not enough, and a stimulant such as senna is usually added; there are no signs of obstruction.
Incorrect. The nurse cannot change a dose without a prescription, and more softener does not stimulate peristalsis.
Incorrect. Fluids and fiber support bowel health, but they act slowly and are not enough for opioid-induced constipation after 3 days without stool.
questions.rationale: Opioids slow the bowel, and stool softeners such as docusate only let water mix into stool so it passes without straining. For opioid-induced constipation, a softener alone is usually not enough, so a stimulant laxative such as senna is usually added. Laxatives are held when obstruction is suspected, but this client is passing flatus, has no vomiting, and has a soft, nontender abdomen. Holding the opioid may seem logical, but it is not the nurse's decision alone and would leave pain uncontrolled.
questions.takeaway: For opioid-induced constipation, a softener alone is usually not enough; collaborate to add a stimulant laxative when there are no signs of obstruction.
questions.hintContent: Compare what a stool softener does with what an opioid does to peristalsis.
questions.hintStrategy: Before choosing a laxative-related action, scan the data for obstruction cues; if none are present, choose the option that matches the cause.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 41-year-old client is admitted with fever of 38.7°C (101.7°F), cramping, and frequent loose stools with streaks of blood that started a day after eating undercooked chicken. The client has a PRN prescription for loperamide and asks for a dose. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Start contact precautions, then give the loperamide
Restrict oral intake to rest the bowel
Give the loperamide with an oral rehydration drink
Consult the provider before giving the loperamide
optionRationales: Incorrect. Contact precautions are appropriate for suspected infectious diarrhea, but they do not make the antidiarrheal safe to give.
Incorrect. Bowel rest is sometimes used for GI illness, but restricting intake worsens fluid loss in a client with fever and diarrhea; fluids should be replaced.
Incorrect. Fluid replacement is appropriate, but it does not make the antidiarrheal safe to give.
Correct. An infectious cause is suspected, and slowing the bowel can hold the germ or its toxin inside, so the nurse checks with the provider first.
questions.rationale: Antidiarrheal agents such as loperamide slow intestinal movement so more water is absorbed. When an infectious cause is suspected, slowing the bowel can hold the germ or its toxin inside, so the nurse checks with the provider before giving it. Fever, blood in the stool, and a history of undercooked food all point to infection. Combining the drug with fluids is tempting because fluid replacement is correct, but the medication itself is the problem.
questions.takeaway: Check with the provider before giving an antidiarrheal when diarrhea may be infectious, such as with fever or blood.
questions.hintContent: Consider what slowing the bowel would do if bacteria or their toxins are causing the diarrhea.
questions.hintStrategy: When a PRN medication is requested, check whether new cues make it unsafe before giving it.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with a 5-day-old ileostomy says the skin around the stoma burns and the pouch has leaked twice today. The nurse removes the pouch and finds red, moist skin and a barrier opening about 1 cm larger than the stoma on all sides. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Re-measure the stoma and cut the barrier to fit closely
Apply barrier cream and put the same pouch back on
Notify the surgeon that the stoma may be infected and needs review
Consult the wound and ostomy nurse about the skin
optionRationales: Correct. The oversized opening lets enzyme-rich stool touch the skin, so the barrier must be refitted to cover the skin closely around the stoma.
Incorrect. Barrier cream helps protect skin, but reusing a pouch with an oversized opening keeps exposing the skin to stool.
Incorrect. The surgeon should be told about stoma problems, but the stoma itself is not described as abnormal, and the skin damage is explained by the poor fit.
Incorrect. The wound and ostomy nurse is a good follow-up resource, but the nurse can fix the poor fit now, and waiting leaves the skin exposed to stool.
questions.rationale: Ileostomy output is liquid and full of digestive enzymes that damage skin quickly. The barrier opening should be cut only slightly larger than the stoma so the skin is covered but the stoma is not squeezed. After surgery, the stoma shrinks as swelling goes down, so it must be measured often and the opening resized. Barrier cream helps protect skin, which makes it tempting, but the cause of the damage is the poor fit, and that must be fixed first; the wound and ostomy nurse can follow up.
questions.takeaway: Peristomal skin damage with leaking usually means a poor barrier fit; re-measure and cut the opening to fit closely.
questions.hintContent: Ask what is allowing stool to touch the skin in the first place.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the action that fixes the cause of the problem over one that only treats its effect.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: An 87-year-old client in long-term care has had six loose stools since morning and is incontinent. The perineal skin is red but intact. Which nursing action is most important?
options: Apply an adult brief and check the client every 2 hours
Report the red skin to the provider for a medicated cream
Clean gently after each stool, pat dry, and apply a barrier cream
Cleanse with a no-rinse cleanser at the end of each shift
optionRationales: Incorrect. Regular checks are helpful, but a brief traps moisture, and stool can sit on the skin for up to 2 hours between checks.
Incorrect. The provider may need to know if skin breaks down, but red, intact skin is managed first with independent nursing hygiene measures.
Correct. Gentle cleansing after every stool, patting dry, and a moisture barrier protect red skin from breaking down.
Incorrect. A no-rinse cleanser is gentle on skin, but cleaning once a shift leaves liquid stool on the skin for hours.
questions.rationale: Personal hygiene is an independent nursing intervention that protects skin and prevents infection. Stool, especially liquid stool, damages skin quickly, so the perineal area is cleansed gently after every stool and patted dry. A moisture barrier cream is applied when skin is often exposed to stool. Briefs, scheduled checks, and gentle cleansers all have a place, but cleaning on a schedule rather than after each stool leaves stool on the skin, and red but intact skin does not need a provider before the nurse acts.
questions.takeaway: With frequent stools, clean gently after every stool, pat dry, and protect the skin with a moisture barrier.
questions.hintContent: Think about what keeps red skin from becoming broken skin.
questions.hintStrategy: When skin is already red, choose the action that removes the irritant promptly and protects the skin.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A medical-surgical nurse receives report on four clients with bowel elimination concerns. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with constipation who is asking for prune juice with breakfast
A client with dementia who was incontinent of soft stool an hour ago
A client with a new colostomy who is tearful and will not look at the stoma
A client with diverticulitis who now has a rigid abdomen and a high fever
optionRationales: Incorrect. This client has a stable, routine need that can wait.
Incorrect. This client needs hygiene care soon, but the problem is not life-threatening.
Incorrect. Body-image concerns matter, but a psychosocial need comes after an acute physiologic problem.
Correct. Inflamed bowel tissue in diverticulitis can perforate, and a rigid abdomen with high fever suggests that complication.
questions.rationale: Inflammation is one of the concepts linked to bowel elimination, and inflamed bowel tissue, as in diverticulitis, can obstruct or perforate. A rigid abdomen with a high fever in that setting suggests perforation, an emergency that needs immediate assessment and provider notification. The other clients have real needs, but they are stable or psychosocial. The tearful ostomy client may tug at the nurse's attention, but emotional support follows physiologic stability.
questions.takeaway: In diverticulitis, a rigid abdomen with fever suggests perforation and takes priority over stable or psychosocial needs.
questions.hintContent: Identify the client whose findings suggest a complication that can quickly become life-threatening.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the acute-versus-chronic and physiologic-before-psychosocial rules to rank multiple clients.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a family whose 35-year-old member is recovering from infectious diarrhea. Two young children live in the home. Which instruction is most important for preventing spread to others?
options: "Clean the toilet, sink, and door handles with a disinfectant once a day."
"Keep the ill person's towels, cups, and dishes separate from everyone else's."
"Everyone should wash hands after using the toilet and before handling food."
"Wipe from front to back after each bowel movement to keep the area clean."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cleaning shared surfaces helps, but germs on hands spread between daily cleanings, so hand hygiene is the most important step.
Incorrect. Separating towels and dishes reduces some spread, but it does not stop germs carried on hands to food and mouths.
Correct. Hand hygiene after toileting and before food preparation breaks the stool-to-mouth spread of infectious diarrhea.
Incorrect. Wiping front to back is correct hygiene, but it protects the ill person from urinary infection rather than preventing spread to others.
questions.rationale: Poor hygiene is a modifiable risk factor because germs spread from stool to mouth and cause infectious diarrhea. Hand hygiene after toileting, and before preparing or eating food, is the key step in preventing spread to others, especially young children. Cleaning surfaces and keeping towels separate also help, but hands are the main route of spread. Wiping front to back protects the person from urinary infection, not the household from diarrhea.
questions.takeaway: Hand hygiene after toileting and before handling food is the key to preventing the spread of infectious diarrhea.
questions.hintContent: Focus on how infectious diarrhea passes from one person to another.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the instruction to the goal named in the stem; here the goal is protecting others in the home.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An 82-year-old resident with moderate dementia has become restless and agitated over the past 2 days and keeps pulling at her brief. Her last recorded bowel movement was 5 days ago. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the PRN antianxiety medication for the new agitation
Assess the abdomen and review the bowel elimination record
Ask the family to visit so they can help calm the resident
Change the brief and check the perineal skin for irritation
optionRationales: Incorrect. New agitation may need treatment, but sedating the resident before assessing for a physical cause could hide constipation or impaction.
Correct. A client with dementia may not recognize or report the urge to defecate, so new agitation with no stool for 5 days calls for a bowel assessment first.
Incorrect. Family support may help, but it does not identify a possible physical cause of the behavior.
Incorrect. A wet brief or sore skin can cause pulling, so checking is reasonable, but it does not address 5 days without a bowel movement.
questions.rationale: Cognition is one of the concepts linked to bowel elimination: a client with dementia may not recognize the urge or be able to tell anyone about discomfort. New restlessness, agitation, and pulling at a brief in a client with no bowel movement for 5 days are cues of constipation or impaction. The nurse assesses the abdomen and reviews the bowel record before treating the behavior. A PRN sedative is tempting because the resident is agitated, but it could mask a treatable physical problem.
questions.takeaway: New agitation in a client with dementia can be a sign of constipation; assess for a physical cause before giving a sedative.
questions.hintContent: Consider how a client with dementia might show bowel discomfort when they cannot describe it.
questions.hintStrategy: When a behavior changes suddenly, assess for a physical cause before choosing a medication or restraint.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 72-year-old client in rehabilitation after a stroke has chronic constipation with irregular bowel movements. Meals are served at 0730, 1200, and 1730, and the client can sit on a commode with help. When should the nurse schedule bowel training?
options: About 30 minutes after breakfast, with a warm drink
First thing on waking in the morning, before any food or fluid
About 30 minutes after the evening meal each day
At a different time each day, whenever the urge occurs
optionRationales: Correct. Eating triggers the gastrocolic reflex, and a warm drink with breakfast adds to it, so the period after breakfast takes advantage of the body's own push.
Incorrect. Before eating, the gastrocolic reflex has not been triggered, so the urge is weaker.
Incorrect. Any meal triggers the gastrocolic reflex, but it is usually strongest after breakfast, which makes the morning the better routine time.
Incorrect. Responding to the urge is good practice, but bowel training relies on a consistent daily time to build a routine.
questions.rationale: Bowel training sets a regular, predictable time for defecation. It works because the bowel responds to routine and to the gastrocolic reflex, the wave of colon activity triggered by eating. The best time is shortly after a meal, often breakfast, with a warm drink, with the client upright on a toilet or commode, given privacy and time. First thing on waking may sound natural, but without food in the stomach the reflex has not yet been triggered.
questions.takeaway: Schedule bowel training shortly after a meal, usually breakfast, to use the gastrocolic reflex.
questions.hintContent: Recall which reflex is triggered by food entering the stomach.
questions.hintStrategy: When choosing a time for a routine, match it to the physiologic trigger the routine depends on.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse is implementing a bowel training program for a stable 79-year-old resident with chronic constipation. Which task is appropriate to delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
options: Teaching the resident why the routine follows a meal
Assessing bowel sounds before each toileting attempt
Helping the resident onto the commode 30 minutes after breakfast
Evaluating after 2 weeks whether the bowel training routine is working
optionRationales: Incorrect. Teaching is a nursing responsibility.
Incorrect. Assessment of bowel sounds requires nursing judgment.
Correct. Assisting a stable resident to the commode at a set time is routine care that AP can perform.
Incorrect. Evaluating the effectiveness of the plan is the nurse's role.
questions.rationale: Bowel training uses a consistent time after a meal, an upright position, privacy, and enough time. Helping a stable resident onto the commode at the scheduled time is routine care that AP can do and report on. Teaching, assessment, and evaluation all require nursing knowledge and judgment and cannot be delegated. Evaluating the routine may seem like simple record-keeping, but deciding whether a plan is effective is a nursing judgment.
questions.takeaway: AP can carry out the toileting schedule; the nurse teaches, assesses, and evaluates the bowel program.
questions.hintContent: Sort the options by whether they require teaching, assessment, or evaluation.
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation items, the delegable task is usually the routine, repeated, hands-on care for a stable client.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 63-year-old client who is starting psyllium for chronic constipation. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "I'll take it with just a sip of water so I don't feel full."
"I'll keep drinking plenty of fluids during the day."
"It works by adding bulk, so it may take a while to help."
"I won't take it if my belly hurts badly and I can't pass gas."
optionRationales: Correct. This statement needs correction: bulk-forming laxatives must be taken with a full glass of water, or they can harden stool and cause blockage.
Incorrect. This is accurate; fluid supplies the water that bulk-forming fiber needs to soften stool.
Incorrect. This is accurate; psyllium adds bulk and does not produce a quick bowel movement.
Incorrect. This is accurate; laxatives are not taken with suspected obstruction or unexplained abdominal pain.
questions.rationale: Psyllium is a bulk-forming laxative that adds bulk and holds water in the stool. It must be taken with a full glass of water, and fluid intake should continue through the day, because fiber without enough fluid can make stool harder and cause blockage. Laxatives are never taken with a suspected obstruction or unexplained abdominal pain. The client's wish to avoid fullness sounds reasonable, which makes it a tempting statement to accept, but too little water defeats the medication.
questions.takeaway: Give bulk-forming laxatives with a full glass of water and keep fluids up through the day.
questions.hintContent: Consider what fiber needs in order to soften stool.
questions.hintStrategy: In "needs further teaching" items, find the statement that would make the treatment unsafe or ineffective.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: During an annual checkup, a 78-year-old client answers "No" when asked, "Any problems?" Which question by the nurse is most likely to identify an elimination problem?
options: "You aren't having any trouble with your bladder or bowels these days, are you?"
"Are your bowels and your bladder working the way you think they should be?"
"How many times a week do you usually have a bowel movement?"
"Many people leak urine or stool. Do you ever leak before reaching the toilet?"
optionRationales: Incorrect. It names both bladder and bowels, which is specific, but the leading wording invites an embarrassed client to simply say no.
Incorrect. This open question seems polite and respectful, but it is vague and lets the client answer without describing any symptoms.
Incorrect. Asking about frequency is a useful, specific question, but it screens only one bowel problem and does not ease the embarrassment that keeps clients from reporting leaking.
Correct. This direct, normalizing question names specific symptoms and makes it easier for an embarrassed client to answer honestly.
questions.rationale: There are no standard screening procedures for elimination problems, so nurses use verbal screening during checkups, especially for older adults. Elimination problems require more direct questioning than other problems, because clients are often embarrassed or believe leaking or constipation is a normal part of aging. A normalizing statement followed by a specific question gets more honest answers. The vague question seems polite and open, but it lets the client answer without describing anything.
questions.takeaway: Screen for elimination problems with direct, normalizing questions that name specific symptoms.
questions.hintContent: Think about why clients may not volunteer bowel or bladder problems.
questions.hintStrategy: For communication items, reject leading and vague questions and choose the one most likely to bring out accurate information.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 47-year-old client with diarrhea from a noninfectious cause has taken loperamide for 3 days. Today the client has had no bowel movement for 36 hours and reports abdominal bloating. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: The medication has worked, so the dose can be continued as it was ordered
The medication may be causing constipation and should be reported
The client may be dehydrated from the diarrhea and needs more fluids
The lack of stool is likely from eating less during the illness
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stopping diarrhea was the goal, but continuing the drug after stool has stopped can lead to constipation.
Correct. Antidiarrheals slow the bowel, and constipation is a known effect, so the finding is reported and the drug is likely held.
Incorrect. Replacing fluids is part of care during diarrhea, but dehydration does not explain new bloating with no stool while on an antidiarrheal.
Incorrect. Low intake can reduce stool, but it does not explain new bloating and overlooks the drug's known constipating effect.
questions.rationale: Antidiarrheal agents such as loperamide slow intestinal movement so more water is absorbed. The nurse watches for constipation as a side effect and keeps replacing fluids while the drug is in use. Thirty-six hours without stool plus bloating suggests the drug has gone too far, so the nurse assesses the abdomen and reports the finding. Thinking the drug simply worked is tempting, but the goal is a return to normal stool, not no stool at all.
questions.takeaway: Watch clients taking antidiarrheals for constipation, and report it when stool stops and bloating begins.
questions.hintContent: Recall the main side effect to monitor with a drug that slows the bowel.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, decide whether the result shows the intended effect or an overshoot into a side effect.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: On the third day after a colostomy, a 54-year-old client turns away during pouch care and says, "I can't even look at it. Who would want to be near me now?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Lots of people have ostomies and live completely normal lives."
"This is a big change. Tell me more about what worries you."
"Let's go over how to change the pouch so you feel in control."
"Don't worry. Once you get used to it, you won't even notice it."
optionRationales: Incorrect. This reassurance compares the client with others and dismisses the client's feelings.
Correct. This response acknowledges the feeling and invites the client to share concerns, which supports grieving the change in body image.
Incorrect. Teaching is important, but the client is not ready to learn while overwhelmed and turning away.
Incorrect. This is false reassurance and cuts off further discussion.
questions.rationale: Many clients grieve the change an ostomy brings to their body, and supporting body image is part of ostomy care. A client who turns away and voices fear of rejection needs the nurse to listen first. An open, empathetic response helps the client express feelings and lets the nurse learn what support is needed, including the wound and ostomy nurse. Jumping into pouch teaching is tempting because self-care is the long-term goal, but learning is unlikely while the client is this upset.
questions.takeaway: When a client grieves a new ostomy, acknowledge the feeling and invite them to talk before teaching.
questions.hintContent: Notice the client's emotional state and readiness to learn.
questions.hintStrategy: In therapeutic communication items, choose the response that acknowledges feelings and opens discussion; reject reassurance and premature teaching.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A nurse reviews prescriptions for four clients. For which client is a stool softener such as docusate most appropriate?
options: A client with distension, vomiting, and no flatus for 2 days
A client with fever and bloody diarrhea after travel
A client who needs a bowel movement within the next hour
A client with hemorrhoids who strains to pass hard stools
optionRationales: Incorrect. These cues suggest obstruction, and medications that promote bowel movements are held.
Incorrect. This client has diarrhea, possibly infectious, and a softener would add to it.
Incorrect. Stool softeners prevent hard stool over time; they do not produce a quick bowel movement.
Correct. Stool softeners are used for clients who should not strain, such as those with hemorrhoids.
questions.rationale: Stool softeners such as docusate let water mix into stool so it is soft and passes without straining. They suit clients who should not strain, including those with hemorrhoids, after surgery or childbirth, or while taking opioids. They prevent hard stool rather than cause a quick bowel movement. A client who needs results within the hour may tempt a student who thinks softeners act fast, but that is the job of other agents ordered by the provider.
questions.takeaway: Stool softeners prevent straining over time; they are not for quick results, diarrhea, or suspected obstruction.
questions.hintContent: Recall how a stool softener works and how quickly it acts.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the drug's mechanism to the client's problem, and eliminate any client for whom the drug is contraindicated.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client is seen 2 weeks after hip surgery under general anesthesia for a work injury. The client has a BMI of 36, eats fast food most days, takes oxycodone and an iron supplement, and has a father who had colon cancer. Which findings are modifiable risk factors for altered bowel elimination? Select all that apply.
options: Recent surgery under general anesthesia
Age of 52 years
Fast food most days
BMI of 36
Father with colon cancer
Daily oxycodone and iron
optionRationales: Correct. Medical procedures that require anesthesia slow peristalsis and can cause constipation or ileus.
Incorrect. Age cannot be changed, so it is not a modifiable risk factor.
Correct. A poor, low-fiber diet is a modifiable risk factor for constipation.
Correct. Obesity is a modifiable risk factor that can be reduced with diet and activity changes.
Incorrect. Family history cannot be changed, so it is not a modifiable risk factor.
Correct. Pharmacologic treatment of other conditions affects the bowel; opioids and iron constipate.
questions.rationale: Modifiable risk factors are those a person can change or that can be reduced. They include obesity, pregnancy, medical procedures requiring anesthesia, medications for other conditions, lower socioeconomic status and education, poor hygiene, poor diet and food handling, and travel. Opioids and iron are classic constipating drugs, and anesthesia slows peristalsis. Family history and age matter for screening, which makes them tempting, but they cannot be changed.
questions.takeaway: Modifiable bowel risk factors include obesity, anesthesia, constipating medications, and poor diet; age and family history are not modifiable.
questions.hintContent: Ask of each finding: could this client or the care team change or reduce it?
questions.hintStrategy: In risk-factor SATA items, separate modifiable from nonmodifiable factors before deciding.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse is writing a plan of care for a 70-year-old client with chronic constipation. Which interventions can the nurse initiate independently, without a provider's order? Select all that apply.
options: Encouraging increased fluid and fiber intake
Ordering a stool culture
Teaching about the effects of dietary choices
Giving a daily stimulant laxative
Starting loperamide if stools become loose
Setting up a bowel training routine after meals
optionRationales: Correct. Encouraging fluid and fiber is a first-line independent intervention.
Incorrect. Diagnostic tests such as a stool culture require a provider's order.
Correct. Diet teaching is an independent nursing intervention.
Incorrect. Laxatives are a collaborative therapy that requires a prescription.
Incorrect. Antidiarrheal agents are a collaborative therapy that requires a prescription.
Correct. Bowel training is an independent nursing intervention.
questions.rationale: Bowel care falls into independent interventions and collaborative therapies. Independent interventions include encouraging fluid and fiber, teaching about diet, bowel training, pelvic floor exercises, personal hygiene, and ostomy care. Collaborative therapies, such as laxatives, stool softeners, antidiarrheals, and surgery, need a provider's order. Diagnostic tests also need an order. Laxatives are tempting because many are sold over the counter, but in a plan of care, giving any medication requires a prescription.
questions.takeaway: Fluid and fiber, diet teaching, bowel training, Kegels, hygiene, and ostomy care are independent; medications and surgery are collaborative.
questions.hintContent: Separate what a nurse can start on nursing judgment from what requires a prescription.
questions.hintStrategy: In scope-of-practice SATA items, any medication option almost always requires an order.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 38-year-old client with constipation says, "I eat white rice and chicken most nights, a lot of cheese, and coffee all day." Which suggestions should the nurse include in teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Choose white bread over whole-grain bread
Swap white rice for brown rice or other whole grains
Eat more cheese to add protein to meals
Add a second serving of chicken at dinner
Snack on fruit such as prunes
Add a vegetable to the evening meal
optionRationales: Incorrect. Highly processed, low-fiber foods such as white bread tend to constipate.
Correct. Whole grains add fiber, which adds bulk and holds water in stool.
Incorrect. Large amounts of cheese tend to constipate.
Incorrect. Large amounts of meat tend to constipate and add no fiber.
Correct. Fruits, especially prunes, help loosen stool.
Correct. Vegetables add fiber and help loosen stool.
questions.rationale: Teaching about dietary choices is an independent nursing intervention that helps clients link food to bowel function. Low-fiber processed foods and large amounts of cheese and meat tend to constipate, while fruits (especially prunes), vegetables, and whole grains loosen stool. Fiber also needs fluid to work, so the nurse encourages water throughout the day. More cheese may sound healthy because of the protein, but it worsens constipation.
questions.takeaway: For constipation, swap processed foods, cheese, and extra meat for whole grains, fruits, and vegetables, with plenty of water.
questions.hintContent: Sort the foods into those that loosen stool and those that tend to constipate.
questions.hintStrategy: In diet-teaching SATA items, check each option against the specific problem named in the stem.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 61-year-old client with a descending colostomy says the pouch fills with gas and is embarrassing at work. Which foods and drinks in the client's diet are most likely contributing? Select all that apply.
options: Baked chicken
Cabbage
Black beans
Carbonated water
White rice
Oatmeal
optionRationales: Incorrect. Plain baked chicken is not a gas-forming food.
Correct. Cabbage is a gas-forming food.
Correct. Beans are gas-forming foods.
Correct. Carbonated drinks add gas to the GI tract.
Incorrect. White rice is not one of the common gas-forming foods.
Incorrect. Oatmeal is not one of the common gas-forming foods.
questions.rationale: Part of ostomy teaching is helping the client know which foods cause gas or odor. Common gas-forming foods are beans, cabbage, onions, and cauliflower, plus carbonated drinks. Knowing these lets the client plan meals around work and social events instead of avoiding food altogether. Oatmeal may seem suspect because it is high in fiber, but it is not among the common gas-formers.
questions.takeaway: Beans, cabbage, onions, cauliflower, and carbonated drinks are the common gas-formers to teach ostomy clients.
questions.hintContent: Recall which foods and drinks are known to produce gas in the GI tract.
questions.hintStrategy: In diet SATA items, judge each item individually instead of assuming every high-fiber food causes the problem.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: The nurse evaluates a 44-year-old client's learning before discharge with a new ileostomy. Which statements show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
options: "I'll wait until the pouch is completely full so I empty it less often."
"I'll drink enough fluid to replace what I lose through the stoma."
"I'll clean the skin around the stoma with warm water and pat it dry."
"I'll cut the barrier opening just slightly larger than my stoma."
"I'll cut the opening extra large so the barrier never touches the stoma."
"I'll empty the pouch when it's about one-third to one-half full."
optionRationales: Incorrect. A full, heavy pouch can pull loose and leak.
Correct. Ileostomy output is liquid, so the client must drink enough to replace losses.
Correct. Warm water and patting dry protect the peristomal skin.
Correct. A close fit covers the skin without squeezing the stoma.
Incorrect. An oversized opening lets enzyme-rich stool touch and damage the skin.
Correct. Emptying at one-third to one-half full prevents a heavy pouch from pulling loose and leaking.
questions.rationale: Ostomy care is an independent nursing intervention, and much of it is teaching the client to manage at home. The pouch is emptied at one-third to one-half full, and the barrier opening is cut to fit closely, only slightly larger than the stoma. The peristomal skin is cleaned with warm water, patted dry, and inspected, and a client with an ileostomy must drink enough fluid to replace losses.
