Cutting the opening extra large sounds protective of the stoma, which makes it tempting, but it exposes the skin to stool.
questions.takeaway: Empty the pouch at one-third to one-half full, cut the barrier to fit closely, and, with an ileostomy, replace lost fluid.
questions.hintContent: For each statement, ask whether it protects the skin, the seal, and the client's fluid balance.
questions.hintStrategy: In teaching-evaluation SATA items, select every statement a nurse would be comfortable hearing the client repeat at home.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A nurse is starting a bowel training program for a 66-year-old client with chronic constipation. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Respond to the urge to defecate without delay
Sit upright on the toilet with feet supported, leaning slightly forward
Use a bedpan in bed because it is more convenient
Use the toilet at the same time every day
Expect a regular pattern within 2 to 3 days
Allow enough private, unhurried time on the toilet
optionRationales: Correct. Ignoring the urge lets stool dry out and weakens the urge over time.
Correct. An upright, forward-leaning position with feet supported uses gravity and makes pushing easier.
Incorrect. A bedpan is used only if there is no other option because the position makes defecation harder.
Correct. Repeating the routine at the same time daily trains the bowel.
Incorrect. Establishing a pattern may take weeks, not days.
Correct. Privacy and enough time help the client relax and defecate.
questions.rationale: Bowel training builds a predictable pattern by using routine and the gastrocolic reflex. The client sits upright on a toilet or commode with feet supported and leaning slightly forward, at the same time each day, with privacy and time. Clients are taught never to ignore the urge, and to keep up fluid, fiber, and activity. Expecting results in a few days is tempting because it encourages the client, but it sets up disappointment, since a pattern may take weeks to develop.
questions.takeaway: Bowel training: same time daily after a meal, upright and supported, private and unhurried, and never ignore the urge.
questions.hintContent: Picture the position and routine that make defecation easiest and most predictable.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject SATA options that set unrealistic time frames or choose convenience over effectiveness.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A nursery nurse reviews the stool log for four newborns shown in the exhibit. Which newborn requires the nurse to notify the provider?
options: Baby A
Baby B
Baby C
Baby D
optionRationales: Incorrect. Passing meconium twice in the first day is expected.
Incorrect. Loose, mustard-yellow, seedy stool is normal for a breastfed infant.
Incorrect. Formula-fed stool is normally pasty and ranges from tan to yellow to green.
Correct. Most newborns pass meconium within 24 hours, and no stool by about 48 hours can signal a blockage or another problem.
questions.rationale: A newborn's first stools are meconium: thick, sticky, and greenish-black. Most newborns pass meconium within the first 24 hours, and a newborn with no stool by about 48 hours should be reported because it can signal a blockage. Baby D is 49 hours old with no stool and a slightly rounded abdomen. Baby B's loose stools might worry a new nurse, but mustard-yellow, seedy, loose stool is normal for a breastfed infant.
questions.takeaway: Report a newborn who has not passed meconium by about 48 hours.
questions.hintContent: Recall when most newborns pass their first stool and when the lack of a stool becomes a concern.
questions.hintStrategy: In exhibit-based newborn items, compare each baby against the expected norm for age and feeding type.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A parent brings a 14-month-old to the emergency department. The child has had bouts of screaming with the knees pulled to the chest every 20 minutes, is sleepy between bouts, has vomited twice, and just passed a red, jelly-like stool. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the provider of the findings immediately
Offer small sips of an oral rehydration drink
Save the stool in a container for testing
Ask the parent when the symptoms first started
optionRationales: Correct. These are classic signs of intussusception, a mechanical obstruction that is an emergency and needs prompt diagnosis and treatment.
Incorrect. Fluid replacement matters after vomiting, but oral fluids are unsafe with a possible obstruction and delay emergency care.
Incorrect. Saving the stool is useful for the provider, but it is not the first action when the cues already point to an emergency.
Incorrect. Onset time is useful history, but the cues already point to an emergency, and more questions delay care.
questions.rationale: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3. One section of intestine telescopes into the next, blocking stool and squeezing the blood supply, so the bowel can die and perforate without treatment. Classic signs are sudden, crampy pain in waves with the knees drawn up, calm or sleepy periods between, vomiting, and currant-jelly stool. Oral rehydration is tempting because the child has vomited, but nothing should be given by mouth when an obstruction is suspected.
questions.takeaway: Episodic screaming with knees to chest, vomiting, and currant-jelly stool in a young child suggests intussusception; notify the provider immediately.
questions.hintContent: Put together the pattern of pain, the vomiting, and the stool appearance in a child under 3.
questions.hintStrategy: When cues point to an emergency, the first action is to get the provider involved rather than treat a single symptom.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client who had a cesarean birth 1 day ago reports sharp, crampy gas pain and a bloated abdomen. Vital signs are stable, and bowel sounds are hypoactive. Which nursing action is most helpful?
options: Give the prescribed opioid to relieve the gas pain
Turn the client onto the left side in bed
Encourage early, frequent walking in the hallway
Ask the provider to prescribe a stool softener
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pain relief is appropriate after surgery, but opioids slow peristalsis and can make gas pain worse.
Incorrect. Lying on the left side can help gas move, but staying in bed keeps peristalsis slow, so it helps less than walking.
Correct. Abdominal surgery and anesthesia slow peristalsis, and early, frequent walking is what helps gas pain most after a cesarean birth.
Incorrect. A stool softener is common after birth and keeps stool soft, but it does not move gas or restore peristalsis.
questions.rationale: Bowels are sluggish after giving birth, and after a cesarean birth, abdominal surgery and anesthesia slow peristalsis further. Gas builds up and causes painful bloating. Early and frequent walking stimulates peristalsis and helps the most. A stool softener is tempting because it is commonly given postpartum, but it addresses hard stool, not trapped gas.
questions.takeaway: After a cesarean birth, early and frequent walking is the best relief for gas pain.
questions.hintContent: Think about why gas builds up after abdominal surgery and what restores bowel movement.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the intervention that treats the cause (slowed peristalsis) over one that treats a different problem.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

rows: No BM for 3 days; eating well; abdomen soft; passing gas
Stools thinner than usual for 6 weeks; no pain
No BM for 6 days; abdomen distended; vomited twice; no flatus today

questions.stem: A charge nurse in a long-term care facility reviews the bowel report in the exhibit at the start of the shift. Which resident should the nurse assess first?
options: Mr. H
Mrs. W
Mr. T
Mrs. E
optionRationales: Incorrect. Three days without a BM in a resident who is eating, passing gas, and has a soft abdomen is not urgent.
Incorrect. A change in stool shape lasting weeks needs referral to the primary care provider, but it is not an acute emergency.
Incorrect. Chronic, stable incontinence with intact skin can be addressed after the acute problem.
Correct. Distension, vomiting, no flatus, and 6 days without stool suggest obstruction or impaction, an acute problem.
questions.rationale: Constipation is common in older adults, but the nurse must separate routine constipation from acute danger. Abdominal distension, vomiting, and no flatus after 6 days without stool are signs of a possible obstruction or impaction that need immediate assessment and provider notification. Thinner stools for 6 weeks are a warning sign that must be referred, which makes Mrs. W tempting, but it is not an emergency this morning. Mr. H and Mr. T are stable.
questions.takeaway: In older adults, distension, vomiting, and no flatus outrank chronic or slowly developing bowel changes.
questions.hintContent: Look for the resident whose bowel may be blocked right now.
questions.hintStrategy: Rank by acuity: an acute, possibly life-threatening problem comes before an important finding that needs a referral.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The parent of an exclusively breastfed 4-month-old calls the clinic. Which report requires the nurse to arrange for the infant to be seen today?
options: Hard, pellet-like stools two or three times over the past week
Spitting up after most feedings while still gaining weight well
A red diaper rash that started once the stools became looser
Watery stools 10 times a day, fewer wet diapers, and a sunken soft spot
optionRationales: Incorrect. Hard stools are unusual in a breastfed infant and are worth discussing, but they are not dangerous and do not need a same-day visit.
Incorrect. Spitting up deserves follow-up, but an infant who is gaining weight is thriving, so this is not urgent.
Incorrect. Diaper rash needs home care teaching, but it is a skin problem, not a threat to fluid balance.
Correct. Frequent watery stools with fewer wet diapers and a sunken fontanel signal dehydration, which develops quickly in infants and needs evaluation today, unlike the other, nonurgent concerns.
questions.rationale: Breastfed infant stools are normally mustard yellow, seedy, soft, and liquid with a faint odor, and frequency varies widely. Parents need to know what is worrying: very watery stools much more often than usual, blood in the stool, or signs of dehydration such as fewer wet diapers, a dry mouth, or a sunken fontanel. Infants dehydrate quickly, so this infant needs to be seen today. Hard stools, spitting up, and diaper rash all deserve teaching or follow-up, but none threatens the infant's fluid balance today.
questions.takeaway: Loose seedy stool is normal for a breastfed infant; watery stools far more often than usual with fewer wet diapers or a sunken fontanel are not.
questions.hintContent: Separate normal breastfed stool features from signs of fluid loss in an infant.
questions.hintStrategy: When most options describe normal variation, choose the one with signs of a physiologic complication.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 77-year-old client takes a stimulant laxative every night "to stay regular" and says it is not working as well as it used to. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Suggest a stool softener in place of the stimulant laxative
Teach the client to drink more water throughout each day
Teach fluid, fiber, and activity, and report the laxative use
Encourage a short walk after each meal to help move the bowel
optionRationales: Incorrect. A softener is gentler, but it keeps the client relying on a drug, and the nurse should not change medications without the provider.
Incorrect. More fluid helps, but it is only one part of the plan and leaves the laxative dependence unaddressed.
Correct. Fluid, fiber, and activity restore natural bowel function, and reporting the laxative use lets the provider help taper it; the other options address only part of the problem.
Incorrect. Activity after meals uses the gastrocolic reflex, but alone it is incomplete and does not address the laxative dependence.
questions.rationale: Laxative use inhibits natural reflexes and may cause constipation rather than relieve it. The bowel comes to depend on the laxative, the client takes more, and the cycle continues. The nurse educates about fluids, fiber, activity, and responding to the gastrocolic reflex after meals, and reports the laxative use so the provider can help taper it. Teaching only water or only walking is tempting because each is correct, but each is incomplete, and swapping to a softener keeps the client dependent on a drug.
questions.takeaway: Laxative overuse in older adults can cause constipation; teach natural measures and report the use instead of increasing the dose.
questions.hintContent: Think about what long-term laxative use does to the bowel's own reflexes.
questions.hintStrategy: Avoid options that do more of the thing causing the problem; choose the one that addresses the cause.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: Right after breakfast, an 83-year-old resident with constipation turns on the call light and tells the assistive personnel (AP), "I need to go now." The AP tells the nurse, "I'll take her after I finish passing breakfast trays." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Ask another AP to help her as soon as someone is free."
"Please help her to the toilet now, and I'll finish the trays."
"Offer her a bedpan in bed so you can keep passing the trays."
"Note her urge on the bowel chart, then help her after trays."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Getting help is reasonable, but waiting for someone to be free delays the response, and the urge may pass.
Correct. The urge after breakfast must be answered right away with the resident upright on a toilet; the nurse removes the barrier by covering the trays instead of delaying or using a bedpan.
Incorrect. A bedpan meets the need quickly, but the upright position on a toilet is far more effective for a constipated older adult.
Incorrect. Tracking bowel patterns is good practice, but documenting first delays toileting and lets the gastrocolic urge fade.
questions.rationale: Responding to the gastrocolic reflex is important for older adults with constipation. The urge to defecate after a meal, especially breakfast, should be answered quickly, with the resident upright on a toilet or commode, so the urge is not lost. Ignoring or delaying the urge lets stool dry out and weakens the urge over time. The bedpan option sounds efficient and still meets the need, which makes it tempting, but the upright position is far more effective.
questions.takeaway: Answer the urge to defecate promptly, especially after breakfast; a delayed urge may be lost.
questions.hintContent: Consider what triggered the urge and what happens to it if the resident waits.
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation items, the nurse can redirect work so the time-sensitive client need is met first.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 15-year-old soccer player reports hard stools every 4 days. He eats fast food most days, drinks mainly sports drinks, and says he "doesn't have time" to use the bathroom at school. Which teaching is the priority?
options: Add fruit, vegetables, whole grains, and water, and don't ignore the urge
Drink water instead of sports drinks during practice and games
Take a daily fiber supplement with a full glass of water each morning
Set aside time to use the toilet at home after breakfast each day
optionRationales: Correct. Fiber, fluid, and responding to the urge address all of this teen's causes: a low-fiber diet, poor fluid intake, and holding stool at school.
Incorrect. Better fluid choices help soften stool, but this addresses only one of his several causes.
Incorrect. A supplement adds fiber, but it does not fix his diet, fluids, or the habit of holding stool.
Incorrect. A routine after breakfast uses the gastrocolic reflex, but it does not address his diet or holding stool during the school day.
questions.rationale: By school age and adolescence, bowel habits are similar to adults', and the same risk factors appear. Diets high in fast food and low in fruits, vegetables, and water, plus holding stool because of busy days or embarrassment, cause constipation. Teaching fiber, fluids, activity, and not ignoring the urge addresses all of this teen's causes. Switching drinks, adding a supplement, or toileting after breakfast are each helpful, but each fixes only one part of the problem.
questions.takeaway: For constipation in children and teens, teach fiber, water, activity, and not ignoring the urge.
questions.hintContent: Identify the specific habits in the stem that are causing hard stools.
questions.hintStrategy: Priority teaching should target the causes named in the stem with first-line, nonmedication measures.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The parent of a 30-month-old says, "She still has accidents, so I make her sit in her room when it happens. Shouldn't she be trained by now?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Let's set up a routine of sitting her on the potty after meals and at bedtime."
"Try a sticker chart along with the time in her room so she learns both ways."
"Training is usually done by 3 to 4 years. Praise works better than punishment."
"Every child trains at her own pace, so try not to compare her with other kids."
optionRationales: Incorrect. A routine helps toilet training, but this response leaves the punishment in place and does not correct the parent's expectation.
Incorrect. Adding praise is good, but continuing the time-outs keeps the punishment, which can lead to stool holding.
Correct. This corrects the expectation with normal development and replaces punishment with praise, addressing both of the parent's problems.
Incorrect. This is supportive, but it does not give the expected age range or address the harmful punishment.
questions.rationale: Some bowel control develops between 18 and 24 months, and successful toilet training is expected by 36 to 48 months. At 30 months, this child is still on track. Parents should use a routine, praise success, and never punish accidents, because pressure and punishment can lead a child to hold stool and become constipated. A potty routine, a sticker chart, or general reassurance each helps a little, but only the best response both corrects the parent's expectation and stops the punishment.
questions.takeaway: Toilet training is usually complete by 36 to 48 months; praise success and never punish accidents.
questions.hintContent: Recall the expected age range for toilet training and what punishment can do to a child's bowel habits.
questions.hintStrategy: In parent-teaching items, choose the response that corrects a misconception and gives a safe, developmentally appropriate approach.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client who is 26 weeks pregnant reports hard stools and bloating and asks, "Should I stop my prenatal vitamins? I read the iron can do this." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Keep taking them, and let's add fluid, fiber, and walking."
"Keep taking them, and swallow each one with a full glass of water."
"Ask your provider about a stool softener so you can keep taking them."
"Constipation is common in pregnancy, and it often eases after birth."
optionRationales: Correct. The prescribed supplement continues, and fluid, fiber, and activity are the first-line way to relieve constipation; the other responses are incomplete or skip nondrug measures.
Incorrect. Continuing the vitamins is right, and water helps, but one glass per dose is too little to relieve constipation.
Incorrect. A softener may be used later, but nondrug measures come first, and this skips them.
Incorrect. This is true, but it offers no help for the client's current discomfort.
questions.rationale: In pregnancy, elevated progesterone relaxes the smooth muscle of the GI tract, slowing gastric emptying and peristalsis, and the growing uterus presses on the intestines. Iron in prenatal vitamins can add to constipation. The answer is not to stop a prescribed supplement but to use fluid, fiber, and activity, and to discuss ongoing problems with the provider. Telling the client constipation is common is true, which makes it tempting, but it offers no help, and a stool softener skips the nondrug measures that come first.
questions.takeaway: Manage pregnancy constipation with fluid, fiber, and activity; do not stop prescribed prenatal vitamins without the provider.
questions.hintContent: Think about all the reasons a pregnant client becomes constipated, not just the iron.
questions.hintStrategy: Avoid options that stop a prescribed medication on the nurse's or client's own decision.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The parent of a 9-year-old says he has had hard, painful stools for a month since starting a new school, where he refuses to use the bathroom. Which explanation by the nurse best describes the likely cause?
options: Starting a new school can bring stress that slows the bowel
School lunches are often low in fiber, which hardens the stool
Children often drink less water during a busy school day
Holding stool lets it dry out and harden, causing constipation
optionRationales: Incorrect. A new school can be stressful, but the stress matters here because it leads him to hold stool, which is the direct cause.
Incorrect. Low fiber can contribute to constipation, but nothing in the report points to a diet change.
Incorrect. Low fluid intake can harden stool, but the key detail is that he refuses to use the school bathroom.
Correct. His refusal to use the school bathroom means he holds stool, which dries out and hardens; the other options are possible contributors the report does not point to.
questions.rationale: By school age, bowel habits are similar to adults', and frequency, quantity, and consistency vary from child to child. Busy days, embarrassment about school bathrooms, or being "too busy" can lead children to hold stool. Held stool dries out and hardens, which causes painful constipation and makes the child want to hold even more. The stress, diet, and fluid options are tempting because each can contribute, but the report points to holding stool as the real cause.
questions.takeaway: Children who hold stool, often to avoid school bathrooms, become constipated; teach them not to ignore the urge.
questions.hintContent: Connect the timing of the problem with the boy's bathroom behavior.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the explanation that links the behavior in the stem to the physiologic result.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A father calls the clinic because his 2-month-old, who is fed formula only, has soft, pasty, green stools. The infant is feeding well and has plenty of wet diapers. How should the nurse interpret this report?
options: The green color suggests a feeding intolerance
This stool is normal for a formula-fed infant
The infant should be switched to a different formula
The stool should be checked for hidden blood
optionRationales: Incorrect. Green stool is within the normal color range for formula feeding and is not a sign of intolerance here.
Correct. Formula-fed stools normally range from tan to yellow to green and are often a bit pastier than breastfed stools.
Incorrect. There is no reason to change formula when the stool is normal and the infant is thriving.
Incorrect. Nothing in the report suggests bleeding.
questions.rationale: Infant stool depends on what the baby is fed. Breastfed stools are mustard yellow and seedy, while formula-fed stools range from tan to yellow to green and are less seedy and more pasty. Both are soft, with a faint odor until solids begin. A well-fed infant with plenty of wet diapers and green, pasty stool is normal, even though parents often worry about the green color.
questions.takeaway: Formula-fed infant stools normally range from tan to yellow to green and are often pasty.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal stool color range for formula-fed infants.
questions.hintStrategy: When an infant is feeding well and well hydrated, a stool difference between feeding types is usually normal variation.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse teaches the mother of a 5-month-old breastfed infant about expected stool changes. Which statement by the mother indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "Her loose, yellow, seedy stools are normal while she's breastfed."
"Once she starts solids, her stool should stay just as loose."
"I should call if I see blood in her diaper."
"Fewer wet diapers or a sunken soft spot would be a reason to call."
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is accurate; loose, mustard-yellow, seedy stool is normal for a breastfed infant.
Correct. This statement needs correction: infant stool becomes firmer and smells stronger once solid foods begin.
Incorrect. This is accurate; blood in the stool should be reported.
Incorrect. This is accurate; these are signs of dehydration that should be reported.
questions.rationale: Infant stools are soft and liquid with a faint odor while the infant is fed breast milk or formula. When solid foods begin, stool becomes firmer and the odor becomes stronger, more like adult stool. Parents should report blood in the stool, very watery stools much more often than usual, or signs of dehydration such as fewer wet diapers or a sunken fontanel. A parent who expects no change may become alarmed when normal firmer, smellier stools appear.
questions.takeaway: Infant stools become firmer and smell stronger once solid foods start.
questions.hintContent: Consider how adding solid food changes the stool.
questions.hintStrategy: In "needs further teaching" items, find the statement that contradicts expected development.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks of gestation asks, "Why am I so constipated now when I never was before?" Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: "Iron in your prenatal vitamin can make your stools harder."
"Pregnancy hormones slow down how fast your bowel moves stool."
"You may be moving around less, which slows down your bowel."
"Hormones slow your bowel, and the growing uterus presses on it."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Iron can add to constipation, but it does not explain why pregnancy itself causes it.
Incorrect. This is true, but incomplete, because it leaves out the pressure of the growing uterus on the bowel.
Incorrect. Inactivity can contribute, but it is not the main reason constipation develops in pregnancy.
Correct. Progesterone relaxes GI smooth muscle and slows peristalsis, and the enlarging uterus presses on the intestines; this is the most complete explanation.
questions.rationale: Elevated progesterone during pregnancy relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body, including the GI tract. This delays gastric emptying and decreases peristalsis, so stool moves more slowly and the colon absorbs more water, leading to bloating and constipation. As the uterus enlarges, it presses on the intestines and aggravates the symptoms. Iron and inactivity can add to the problem, and the hormone effect alone is only half the story, which makes these options tempting for a student who knows part of the mechanism.
questions.takeaway: In pregnancy, progesterone slows the bowel and the enlarging uterus presses on it, causing constipation.
questions.hintContent: Recall the hormone that rises in pregnancy and what it does to smooth muscle.
questions.hintStrategy: For pathophysiology items, trace the mechanism step by step and reject options that reverse it.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: The daughter of an 86-year-old client tells the nurse, "Mom has had bowel accidents a few times a week for the past month. I guess that just happens at her age." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "These accidents aren't normal aging. Her provider should evaluate them."
"Yes, it's common at her age. Adult briefs will help keep her dry."
"Taking her to the toilet after meals may help cut down on accidents."
"More fiber and fluid in her diet may help her bowels become regular."
optionRationales: Correct. New bowel incontinence is not normal aging and often has a treatable cause, so the nurse corrects the belief and refers for evaluation before choosing treatment.
Incorrect. Briefs are practical, but this accepts the incontinence as normal and manages the symptom without finding the cause.
Incorrect. Toileting after meals is a useful strategy, but treating before the cause is evaluated could miss impaction or a neurologic change.
Incorrect. Fiber and fluid often help bowel control, but starting treatment without evaluation could miss a serious cause.
questions.rationale: Bowel incontinence is not a normal part of aging. It usually signals another problem, such as impaction, a neurologic change, or medication effects, that can often be treated. Families often accept it as "just getting older," so the nurse gently corrects that belief and refers the client for evaluation. Offering briefs feels helpful and practical, which makes it tempting, but it manages the symptom without addressing why the incontinence started.
questions.takeaway: Fecal incontinence is never a normal part of aging; refer for evaluation rather than just supplying briefs.
questions.hintContent: Recall whether bowel incontinence is considered part of normal aging.
questions.hintStrategy: When a family member normalizes a new symptom in an older adult, the best response corrects the belief and moves toward evaluation.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: On the first day after a vaginal birth with a second-degree perineal tear, a client says, "I'm scared to have a bowel movement. It's going to hurt so much." Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage walking as tolerated
Give the stool softener if prescribed
Advise her to delay the bowel movement until the stitches heal
Encourage fluids and high-fiber foods
Give the prescribed pain medication
optionRationales: Correct. Walking stimulates peristalsis, which is sluggish after birth.
Correct. A stool softener helps a client who should not strain after childbirth.
Incorrect. Delaying lets stool harden, which makes the next bowel movement more painful.
Correct. Fluid and fiber keep stool soft so the first bowel movement is less painful.
Correct. Controlling perineal pain reduces the fear that leads to delaying elimination.
questions.rationale: Bowels are sluggish after giving birth because of labor, decreased intake, and stretched abdominal muscles. Pain from a tear, stitches, or hemorrhoids can make a new mother afraid to have a bowel movement, and delaying lets stool harden and makes the next one more painful. The nurse gives pain medication, encourages fluid, fiber, and walking, and gives a stool softener as ordered. Advising her to wait sounds kind, but it feeds the cycle of hard, painful stool.
questions.takeaway: After birth, treat pain and keep stool soft with fluid, fiber, walking, and a softener as ordered; never advise delaying.
questions.hintContent: Think about what happens to stool when a client delays a bowel movement out of fear.
questions.hintStrategy: In comfort-and-safety SATA items, reject any option that would worsen the underlying cycle, even if it sounds gentle.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A home health nurse assesses an 81-year-old client with chronic constipation. Which findings are likely contributing to the problem? Select all that apply.
options: Avoids raw fruits because of loose dentures
Takes an opioid for arthritis pain
Walks to the mailbox and back twice a day
Eats oatmeal with prunes every morning
Limits drinks to avoid leaking urine
Spends most of the day sitting in a recliner
optionRationales: Correct. Dental problems that make fruits and vegetables hard to chew reduce fiber intake.
Correct. Medication side effects, including opioids, slow the bowel.
Incorrect. Regular walking stimulates peristalsis and helps prevent constipation.
Incorrect. Oatmeal and prunes are soft, high-fiber foods that help prevent constipation.
Correct. Limiting fluids to avoid incontinence is a common cause of inadequate fluid intake.
Correct. Reduced activity slows peristalsis.
questions.rationale: Constipation is common in older adults for four main reasons: reduced activity, inadequate fluid and fiber, muscle weakness, and medication side effects. Many older adults limit fluids to avoid incontinence, and dental problems can make fruits and vegetables hard to chew. Opioids slow the bowel, so the nurse reviews the medication list and reports contributing drugs. The walking and the oatmeal with prunes are protective, so selecting them would mean reading every detail as a problem.
questions.takeaway: Older adults become constipated from low activity, low fluid and fiber, muscle weakness, and medications.
questions.hintContent: Sort each finding into one that slows the bowel or one that helps it.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA items with mixed findings, some options are protective; do not select them just because they mention bowel habits.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse is triaging an 18-month-old whose parent reports sudden attacks of abdominal pain since this morning. Which findings would support a suspicion of intussusception? Select all that apply.
options: Bouts of crying with the knees drawn up to the chest
Seems calm or sleepy between episodes of pain
Stool mixed with blood and mucus
Steady, mild pain that does not change
Vomiting
Mustard-yellow, seedy stools
optionRationales: Correct. Sudden, severe, crampy pain in waves with the knees drawn to the chest is classic.
Correct. The child may seem calm or sleepy between episodes.
Correct. "Currant jelly" stool, a mix of blood and mucus, is a classic, usually later sign.
Incorrect. The pain of intussusception comes in severe waves, not as a steady, mild ache.
Correct. Vomiting is a classic sign of the obstruction.
Incorrect. Mustard-yellow, seedy stool describes normal breastfed infant stool.
questions.rationale: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3. The pain comes in sudden, severe waves, with screaming and knees pulled to the chest, followed by calm or sleepy periods. Vomiting occurs, and "currant jelly" stool of blood and mucus is a classic later sign; sometimes a sausage-shaped lump can be felt. The calm periods can mislead families and nurses into thinking the child has improved, but they are part of the pattern.
questions.takeaway: Intussusception: severe pain in waves with knees to chest, calm between, vomiting, and currant-jelly stool.
questions.hintContent: Picture what happens each time the bowel telescopes and squeezes, and what comes out when its blood supply is pinched.
questions.hintStrategy: For a condition with a classic pattern, select every option that fits the pattern, including the ones that seem reassuring.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The parent of a 22-month-old asks whether the child is ready to start toilet training. Which observations would indicate readiness? Select all that apply.
options: Can walk to the toilet and sit on it
Can count to five without help
Tells the parent when he needs to go
Stays dry for a couple of hours at a time
Is the same age his older sister was when trained
optionRationales: Correct. Being able to walk to the toilet and sit shows physical readiness.
Incorrect. Counting is a cognitive skill unrelated to toileting readiness.
Correct. Being able to tell a parent about the need to go is a key readiness sign.
Correct. Staying dry for a couple of hours shows growing bladder and sphincter control.
Incorrect. Readiness depends on the child's own signs, not on a sibling's timeline.
questions.rationale: Some bowel control develops at 18 to 24 months as the nerves and muscles of the anal sphincter mature, and successful training is expected by 36 to 48 months. Readiness signs include being able to walk to the toilet, sit, pull pants down, stay dry for a couple of hours, show interest, and tell a parent about the need to go. Physical readiness must come before practice works. Comparing with a sibling feels natural to parents, but each child's readiness is individual.
questions.takeaway: Start toilet training when the child shows readiness signs, not by a set date or a sibling's timeline.
questions.hintContent: Think about what physical and communication skills a child needs to use the toilet.
questions.hintStrategy: Readiness items reward observable signs in the child; reject options based on other people's timelines or unrelated skills.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A clinic nurse reviews health histories of older adult clients. Which reports should the nurse refer to the primary care provider for further evaluation? Select all that apply.
options: A 76-year-old with blood in the stool for 2 weeks
A 73-year-old with new episodes of bowel incontinence
A 70-year-old with new constipation lasting 5 weeks
A 79-year-old with one hard stool after a day of low fluid intake
A 68-year-old with a bowel movement every other day for years
optionRationales: Correct. Blood in the stool is a warning sign that needs evaluation.
Correct. Bowel incontinence is not a normal part of aging and usually signals another problem.
Correct. A change in bowel habits lasting weeks should be referred, because it can be an early sign of colorectal cancer.
Incorrect. A single hard stool with an obvious cause is not a lasting change in bowel habits.
Incorrect. A stable, lifelong pattern within the normal range is not a change.
questions.rationale: In older adults, a change in bowel habits lasting weeks should be referred to the primary care provider. New constipation, new diarrhea, narrower stools, or blood in the stool can be an early sign of a serious problem such as colorectal cancer, whose risk rises with age. Bowel incontinence is not a normal part of aging. A lifelong every-other-day pattern and a single hard stool after low intake may look like "constipation," but neither is a lasting change from the client's own norm.
questions.takeaway: Refer any change in an older adult's bowel habits that lasts weeks, any blood in the stool, and new bowel incontinence.
questions.hintContent: Ask of each report: is this a lasting change from the client's own normal pattern?
questions.hintStrategy: In referral SATA items, separate stable long-standing patterns and one-time events from new, persistent changes.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A nurse is planning care for a 91-year-old long-term care resident with chronic constipation who uses a walker. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Give a stimulant laxative every night to keep her regular
Offer fluids regularly throughout the day
Answer the call light promptly when she needs to go
Assist the resident to the toilet shortly after breakfast
Restrict fluids after lunch to reduce incontinence
optionRationales: Incorrect. Routine laxative use inhibits natural reflexes and can worsen constipation.
Correct. Older adults often have reduced thirst, so fluids are offered regularly.
Correct. Prompt response keeps the urge from being lost.
Correct. Toileting after breakfast takes advantage of the gastrocolic reflex.
Incorrect. Limiting fluids is a common cause of constipation in older adults.
questions.rationale: Older adults are prone to constipation from reduced activity, low fluid and fiber, muscle weakness, and medications. Responding to the gastrocolic reflex is important, so the nurse helps the resident to the toilet after meals, especially breakfast, and answers call lights quickly. Fluids are offered regularly because thirst is reduced. A nightly laxative may seem like a reliable fix, but routine use inhibits the bowel's own reflexes and can make constipation worse.
questions.takeaway: For older adults with constipation, use the gastrocolic reflex, answer call lights promptly, and offer fluids regularly instead of relying on laxatives.
questions.hintContent: Think about what helps an older bowel work on its own.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject SATA options that create dependence or restrict something the body needs.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A pediatric clinic nurse reviews notes from several well-child visits. Which findings are expected for the child's age and feeding? Select all that apply.
options: A 3-day-old who has not yet passed any stool
A 19-month-old who is beginning to show some bowel control
A 3-month-old formula-fed infant with green, pasty stools
A 2-week-old breastfed infant with mustard-yellow, seedy stools
A 6-year-old who has never been toilet trained for stool
optionRationales: Incorrect. Most newborns pass meconium within 24 hours, and none by about 48 hours should be reported.
Correct. Some bowel control is expected between 1.5 and 2 years.
Correct. Formula-fed stool normally ranges from tan to yellow to green and is pasty.
Correct. Mustard-yellow, seedy stool is normal for a breastfed infant.
Incorrect. Successful toilet training is expected by 36 to 48 months, so this child needs evaluation.
questions.rationale: What counts as normal changes with age. Breastfed infants have mustard-yellow, seedy stools, and formula-fed infants have tan to yellow to green, pastier stools. Some bowel control appears at 1.5 to 2 years, and toilet training is usually complete by 36 to 48 months. A 6-year-old who has never been trained and a 3-day-old who has never stooled are both outside the expected range, even though each might be brushed off as "late bloomer" or "slow start."
questions.takeaway: Know the age norms: seedy yellow breastfed stools, tan-to-green formula stools, early control at 18–24 months, training by 36–48 months, meconium by 24 hours.
questions.hintContent: Compare each finding with the expected norm for that age and feeding type.
questions.hintStrategy: In lifespan SATA items, check each age against its milestone before deciding.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Assistive personnel (AP) report that a 78-year-old man admitted with pneumonia "keeps wetting himself. I've changed his pad four times since 0700, but it's only ever a little bit." He has a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the AP to apply an external condom catheter to keep him dry
Check his perineal skin for redness from the wet pads
Assess for bladder distension with a bladder scan
Have the AP offer him a urinal every 2 hours
optionRationales: Incorrect. A condom catheter keeps him dry, but it hides the retention that is likely causing the dribbling.
Incorrect. Skin checks matter with frequent wetness, but skin breakdown is a lower priority than possible urinary retention.
Correct. Frequent small leaks in a man with BPH suggest overflow from retention, so the nurse first checks for a full bladder; the other actions manage wetness or skin without finding the cause.
Incorrect. Scheduled toileting is helpful for some incontinence, but it does not address a bladder that cannot empty.
questions.rationale: Overflow incontinence happens when an outlet obstruction, such as an enlarged prostate, or a weak detrusor keeps the bladder from emptying. The bladder overfills, pressure rises, and urine dribbles out in small amounts. Overflow incontinence is really retention in disguise: the client is wet, but the bladder is full. The nurse assesses with a bladder scan and notifies the provider rather than only managing the wetness; the condom catheter is tempting because it keeps him dry, but it hides the real problem.
questions.takeaway: Frequent small dribbles in a client with BPH suggest overflow from retention; assess the bladder before managing the wetness.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the pattern of frequent, small amounts of urine suggests in a man with an enlarged prostate.
questions.hintStrategy: When AP report a symptom, the nurse's first step is usually to assess the client before choosing an intervention.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman who has always been continent has had three episodes of urinary incontinence since yesterday. Today she is newly confused, her temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), and she says it burns when she voids. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Start scheduled toileting every 2 hours around the clock
Apply an adult brief and monitor for skin breakdown
Begin bladder training today to lengthen her voiding interval
Report the findings to the provider as a possible acute cause
optionRationales: Incorrect. Scheduled toileting manages the symptom without addressing the likely infection.
Incorrect. Containment ignores the acute cause behind the sudden change.
Incorrect. Bladder training is a long-term behavior therapy and is not appropriate for an acute infection.
Correct. New, sudden incontinence with fever, burning, and acute confusion suggests a UTI or another acute cause that must be evaluated.
questions.rationale: Urinary incontinence is a symptom, never a normal part of aging, so the nurse looks for its cause. A UTI irritates the bladder wall, causing urgency and frequency, and is listed as a risk factor for incontinence. In an older adult, new incontinence with burning, fever, or acute confusion should be reported rather than assumed to be aging. Behavior therapies such as scheduled toileting are tempting because they are first-line for chronic incontinence, but they do not fit a sudden change with signs of infection.
questions.takeaway: New, sudden incontinence with fever, burning, or confusion in an older adult signals an acute cause such as UTI; report it.
questions.hintContent: Notice how quickly this change happened and what other new findings came with it.
questions.hintStrategy: Distinguish acute from chronic: a sudden change with new symptoms needs evaluation before long-term management.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A clinic nurse returns four phone calls from clients with incontinence. Which client should the nurse call first?
options: A 44-year-old woman with stress incontinence who wants to learn Kegel exercises
An 80-year-old woman with functional incontinence asking about a bedside commode
A 71-year-old man with BPH who has not voided in 12 hours and has abdominal pain
A 57-year-old man with urge incontinence who wakes twice a night to void
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is a teaching need that can safely wait.
Incorrect. This is an equipment request for a chronic problem.
Correct. No urine for 12 hours with abdominal pain in a man with BPH suggests acute urinary retention, which needs prompt care.
Incorrect. Nocturia with urge incontinence is a chronic, stable problem.
questions.rationale: Prioritization means finding the client with an acute, potentially dangerous problem. BPH can squeeze the urethra and block urine flow, and an outlet obstruction can progress from overflow dribbling to complete retention. A man who has not voided in 12 hours and has abdominal pain needs to be seen right away for bladder decompression. The other clients have chronic, stable incontinence; the nocturia caller may seem pressing because of the sleep disruption, but it is not dangerous.
questions.takeaway: In a client with BPH, inability to void with abdominal pain is acute retention and outranks chronic incontinence concerns.
questions.hintContent: Look for the client whose bladder may not be emptying at all.
questions.hintStrategy: Among several incontinence calls, the acute, painful problem with a physical risk comes first.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a 74-year-old man with left-sided weakness after a stroke. He is continent when his wife helps him, but he is wet most mornings because he cannot reach the bathroom at night. Which intervention should the nurse recommend first?
options: Limit his fluids in the 2 hours before bedtime
Place a bedside commode and a night-light by his bed
Suggest absorbent briefs to keep his bed dry at night
Teach bladder training to lengthen his voiding interval
optionRationales: Incorrect. Limiting evening fluids can reduce night voiding, but it does not solve his inability to reach the bathroom.
Correct. His bladder works, and the problem is access, so a nearby commode and lighting address the cause; the other options reduce or contain urine without fixing access.
Incorrect. Briefs protect the bed, but they contain the problem rather than helping him stay continent.
Incorrect. Bladder training targets urge incontinence, not a mobility barrier that keeps him from the toilet.
questions.rationale: Functional incontinence means the urinary system works, but the client cannot respond to the need in time because of dementia, disability, or impaired mobility. This client is continent with help, so the problem is access, not the bladder. Therapy focuses on the environment: a bedside commode, a clear path, night-lights, assistive devices, and nonrestrictive clothing. Bladder training is tempting because it is a familiar first-line therapy, but it targets urge incontinence, not a mobility barrier.
questions.takeaway: Functional incontinence is fixed by improving access: commode, clear lit path, assistive devices, and easy clothing.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether his bladder or his ability to get to the toilet is the problem.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the intervention to the type of incontinence; for functional incontinence, change the environment.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

tabs.title: Night Shift Notes
tabs.html: Night 1: Found incontinent of urine at 0230; did not wake to void. Night 2: Found incontinent at 0300; drowsy, difficult to rouse fully. Continent during the day. No dysuria; afebrile.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client has been incontinent of urine during the night for 2 nights but is continent during the day. The nurse reviews the exhibit. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Ask the provider if the diuretic can be given in the morning
Apply an adult brief at bedtime to protect the bedding
Wake the client to void at midnight and again at 0400
Ask the provider to order a urinalysis for infection
optionRationales: Correct. Giving furosemide at 2000 fills the bladder overnight while the sedated client cannot wake; moving it to morning fixes the cause, while the other options manage wetness or look for an unlikely cause.
Incorrect. A brief protects the bedding, but it manages the symptom without addressing the medication timing.
Incorrect. Night toileting may reduce accidents, but it disrupts sleep and leaves the evening diuretic in place.
Incorrect. UTI is a common cause, but this client has no signs of infection, and the medication timing explains the pattern.
questions.rationale: Diuretics and sedatives are both listed risk factors for incontinence. A diuretic increases urine volume, and a sedative dulls the sensation of a full bladder and slows the client's response. Here the furosemide is scheduled at 2000 and the temazepam at 2200, so the bladder fills overnight while the client is too drowsy to wake, and incontinence occurs only at night. A urinalysis is tempting because UTI is a common cause, but this client has no signs of infection, and the nurse can address the timing with the provider.
questions.takeaway: Nighttime incontinence in a client taking an evening diuretic and a sedative points to medication timing; collaborate to move the diuretic to the morning.
questions.hintContent: Compare the medication times with the times the client was found wet.
questions.hintStrategy: In MAR exhibits, look for a timing pattern that links a drug to the problem, then choose the action that fixes the cause.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman tells the clinic nurse, "I wear pads all the time now and I've stopped going to church, but leaking is just part of getting old. My mother had it too." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Many women your age have this, so pads are a good way to manage the leaking."
"Kegel exercises can strengthen the muscles that help stop the leaking."
"Leaking is common, but it isn't a normal part of aging. Treatments can help."
"Cutting back on coffee and tea during the day may help reduce the leaking."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pads are practical, but this accepts the leaking as normal and does nothing to address the cause or her isolation.
Incorrect. Kegels help some types of incontinence, but recommending them before evaluation skips correcting her belief and identifying the type.
Correct. This corrects the belief that leaking is normal aging and opens the door to evaluation and treatment, which the other responses skip.
Incorrect. Limiting caffeine can reduce urgency, but this offers a fix before correcting her belief or evaluating the cause.
questions.rationale: Urinary incontinence is a symptom of impaired bladder control, not a normal consequence of aging. It is common in older adults, but common does not mean normal, and treatments exist. It also has a psychosocial impact: clients feel shame, avoid social events, and can become isolated. The best response gently corrects the belief and leads to evaluation, rather than simply supplying more pads; the pad option sounds supportive and practical, which is why it tempts.
questions.takeaway: Incontinence is common but never a normal part of aging; correct the belief and refer for evaluation.
questions.hintContent: Consider whether incontinence is a normal part of aging and how it is affecting her life.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client normalizes a symptom, the best response gently corrects the belief and moves toward help.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 47-year-old client with multiple sclerosis says, "When I have to go, the urge hits me all at once, and I don't make it to the bathroom in time." Which type of incontinence do these findings most likely describe?
options: Urge incontinence
Reflex incontinence
Overflow incontinence
Functional incontinence
optionRationales: Correct. The client feels a strong, sudden urge and cannot hold it, which is the hallmark of urge incontinence.
Incorrect. Reflex incontinence causes urine loss with no urge at all, but this client clearly feels the urge.
Incorrect. Overflow causes dribbling from an overfull bladder, not a sudden strong urge.
Incorrect. Functional incontinence involves a working bladder with a barrier to reaching the toilet, which is not described.
questions.rationale: The key to telling the types apart is asking what triggers the leak and whether the client feels it coming. Urge incontinence comes from an overactive detrusor, so the client feels a strong, sudden urge and cannot hold it. Reflex incontinence, seen with MS or spinal cord injury, causes urination without the urge, a sudden loss with no warning. The diagnosis of MS makes reflex incontinence tempting, but the client's report of feeling the urge points to urge incontinence.
questions.takeaway: Urge incontinence: the client feels the urge but cannot hold it. Reflex incontinence: no urge at all.
questions.hintContent: Focus on whether the client feels the need to void before the leak.
questions.hintStrategy: When a diagnosis suggests one answer, check whether the symptoms actually match it; base the choice on the client's description.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: After hearing she has stress incontinence, a 39-year-old client says, "That can't be right. I'm not stressed at all." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Stress incontinence is very common and can be treated with exercises."
"Kegel exercises can strengthen the muscles that are causing the leaks."
"Your provider can explain the results to you in more detail."
"Here, 'stress' means physical strain, like coughing or lifting."
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is true and reassuring, but it does not correct her misunderstanding of the word stress.
Incorrect. Kegels are first-line teaching, but this skips the client's confusion about her diagnosis.
Incorrect. The provider can add detail, but the nurse can and should clarify this simple point now.
Correct. This directly corrects the misunderstanding: stress means physical pressure that pushes urine past a weak urethra, not emotional stress.
questions.rationale: Stress incontinence has nothing to do with emotional stress. The pelvic muscles have relaxed and the urethra is weak, so urethral resistance is decreased. Anything that raises abdominal and bladder pressure, such as sneezing, coughing, lifting, pregnancy, or obesity, pushes urine past the weak seal. Reassurance, Kegel teaching, and referral to the provider are all reasonable, but only the best response answers the client's actual confusion about the word stress, and Kegels follow once she understands.
questions.takeaway: "Stress" incontinence means physical strain (cough, sneeze, lift), not emotional stress.
questions.hintContent: Think about what kind of "stress" pushes urine past a weak urethra.
questions.hintStrategy: Watch for terms whose medical meaning differs from everyday meaning; the best response clarifies the term.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client reports, "I leak a little when I cough or pick up my grandson, and some days I also get a sudden urge and can't make it to the bathroom." Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?
options: The client has stress incontinence from weak pelvic floor muscles
The client has features of both stress and urge incontinence
The client has urge incontinence from an overactive bladder muscle
The client has overflow incontinence from a bladder that won't empty
optionRationales: Incorrect. Leaking with coughing or lifting does point to stress incontinence, but this ignores her sudden urges.
Correct. She describes two distinct triggers, physical strain and a sudden urge, which together indicate mixed incontinence.
Incorrect. Sudden urges do point to urge incontinence, but this ignores her leaking with coughing and lifting.
Incorrect. Overflow causes frequent dribbling from a full bladder, and nothing in her report suggests retention.
questions.rationale: Some clients have both stress and urge incontinence, which is called mixed incontinence, so the nurse asks about both triggers. Leaks with coughing or lifting point to a weak urethra and decreased urethral resistance. Leaks with a sudden, strong urge point to an overactive detrusor. Students often force a single type onto a client, which makes the stress-only and urge-only options tempting, but each captures only half of what this client describes.
questions.takeaway: Ask about every trigger: leaks with strain plus leaks with urgency mean mixed incontinence.
questions.hintContent: Identify each trigger the client describes and match each to a type.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client describes two different patterns, consider that both may be present rather than choosing just one.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks of gestation says, "I never leaked before, but now I wet myself a little every time I sneeze." Which explanation by the nurse best describes why this is happening?
options: "Pregnancy makes your bladder muscle squeeze on its own without warning."
"The growing uterus presses on your bladder and raises its pressure."
"Your kidneys are making less urine, so the bladder becomes irritated."
"Pregnancy hormones make the urethra tighter, so urine backs up."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Squeezing with no warning describes reflex incontinence from neurologic damage.
Correct. The weight of the growing uterus raises bladder pressure, so a sneeze can push bladder pressure above urethral pressure.
Incorrect. Pregnancy does not reduce urine production in a way that explains leaking with a sneeze.
Incorrect. Pregnancy hormones relax supporting tissue rather than tightening the urethra.
questions.rationale: The pathophysiology of incontinence is a pressure contest: urine escapes when bladder pressure exceeds urethral pressure. In pregnancy, the growing uterus presses down on the bladder from above, and hormonal changes relax the supporting tissue. A sneeze adds a sudden burst of abdominal pressure that pushes urine past the urethra. The option about a tighter urethra reverses the real hormonal effect, which makes it a trap for students who remember hormones but not their direction.
questions.takeaway: In pregnancy, the uterus raises bladder pressure, so strain such as a sneeze can push urine past the urethra.
questions.hintContent: Use the idea of bladder pressure versus urethral pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: For "why" questions, choose the option that correctly explains the mechanism, and reject any that reverse it.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

rows: 4 cups of coffee (morning); 2 cans of caffeinated diet soda (afternoon)
About half of the day's fluid taken after 1900
Every 60–90 min while awake; up 3 times at night
2–3 per day, each with a sudden strong urge

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client with urge incontinence brings a bladder diary to the clinic. The nurse reviews the summary in the exhibit. Which findings are likely contributing to the client's symptoms? Select all that apply.
options: About half of the fluid taken after 1900
Four cups of coffee each morning
Total daily fluid intake of 900 mL
Soft, formed stool every day
Walking for 30 minutes every day
Two cans of caffeinated diet soda each afternoon
optionRationales: Correct. Heavy evening intake contributes to nocturia; fluids should be tapered at night.
Correct. Caffeine is a bladder irritant that triggers contractions.
Correct. Low intake makes urine concentrated, which irritates the bladder wall and increases urgency.
Incorrect. Soft daily stool means constipation, a risk factor for incontinence, is not present.
Incorrect. Regular exercise is part of prevention, not a cause of urgency.
Correct. Diet soda contains caffeine and artificial sweeteners, both bladder irritants.
questions.rationale: Many clients with incontinence limit fluids, but concentrated urine irritates the bladder lining, so the detrusor contracts more often and urgency gets worse. The goal is more than 2,000 mL/day, spaced through the day, with less at night to prevent nocturia. Caffeine and artificial sweeteners are bladder irritants. Walking and soft daily stool are protective, so selecting them would mean treating every diary entry as a problem.
questions.takeaway: Low total fluid, bladder irritants, and heavy evening intake worsen urge incontinence and nocturia.
questions.hintContent: Compare the diary with the prevention guidance for fluid amount, fluid timing, and irritants.
questions.hintStrategy: In exhibit SATA items, check every row against the standard; some rows show healthy behavior and should not be selected.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse reviews the histories of six clients with urinary incontinence. Which clients are most likely to have overflow incontinence? Select all that apply.
options: A 41-year-old woman who leaks when she sneezes or jumps
An 85-year-old with dementia who cannot find the bathroom
A 52-year-old with a stone lodged at the bladder outlet who dribbles urine
A 76-year-old man with BPH who dribbles urine all day
A 68-year-old with a weak detrusor muscle and a distended bladder
A 33-year-old with a spinal cord injury who wets with no urge
optionRationales: Incorrect. Leaking with sneezing or jumping is stress incontinence.
Incorrect. A working bladder with an inability to reach the toilet is functional incontinence.
Correct. A stone (calculus) blocking the bladder outlet obstructs urine flow, so the bladder overfills and dribbles.
Correct. BPH can squeeze the urethra, so the bladder overfills and urine dribbles out.
Correct. A weak detrusor cannot empty the bladder, so it overfills and leaks.
Incorrect. Wetting with no urge from nerve damage is reflex incontinence.
questions.rationale: Overflow incontinence happens when either the outlet is blocked or the detrusor is too weak to empty. Urine builds up, the bladder overfills, and urine dribbles out. Causes include an overdistended bladder, retention, urinary obstruction such as calculi, and BPH. The spinal cord injury client is a tempting pick because neurologic bladders can retain urine, but wetting with no urge is the classic description of reflex incontinence.
questions.takeaway: Overflow incontinence comes from an outlet obstruction (BPH, stones) or a weak detrusor; the bladder overfills and dribbles.
questions.hintContent: For each client, ask whether the bladder is failing to empty.
questions.hintStrategy: In type-matching SATA items, use the classic clue for each type to rule options in or out.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A nurse is completing a holistic assessment of a 72-year-old client who has had urinary incontinence for 2 years. Which findings would the nurse recognize as possible consequences of the incontinence? Select all that apply.
options: A fall last month while rushing to the bathroom at night
A rash and reddened skin in the perineal area
Reports feeling sad and "not wanting to see anyone"
No longer attends her weekly card group
Blood pressure of 128/76 mm Hg
optionRationales: Correct. Clients may fall as they rush to the bathroom at night.
Correct. Wet skin breaks down, and rashes and infections develop.
Correct. Clients can become isolated or depressed.
Correct. Clients often avoid social events because they fear leaking.
Incorrect. A normal blood pressure is not a consequence of incontinence.
questions.rationale: Urinary incontinence has both physical and psychosocial effects. Physically, wet skin breaks down, rashes and infections develop, and clients may fall as they rush to the bathroom at night. Psychosocially, clients feel shame, avoid social events, limit exercise and intimacy, and can become isolated or depressed, and depression itself raises the risk of incontinence. Skin and falls are easy to spot, but the social withdrawal and sadness are just as important to recognize.
questions.takeaway: Incontinence causes physical harm (skin breakdown, falls) and psychosocial harm (shame, isolation, depression).
questions.hintContent: Think about how leaking affects the skin, safety, social life, and mood.
questions.hintStrategy: In holistic-assessment SATA items, include both physical and psychosocial consequences.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 50-year-old client has stress incontinence. Which factors in her history most likely contribute to this type of incontinence? Select all that apply.
options: A BMI of 35
A chronic cough from smoking
An overactive detrusor muscle
A cystocele found on pelvic exam
A spinal cord injury at T10
optionRationales: Correct. Extra abdominal weight presses constantly on the bladder.
Correct. A chronic cough repeatedly strains the pelvic floor and raises bladder pressure.
Incorrect. An overactive detrusor causes urge incontinence, not stress incontinence.
Correct. A cystocele (bladder prolapse) adds pressure and weakens support, decreasing urethral resistance.
Incorrect. Neurologic damage causes reflex incontinence, with loss and no urge.
questions.rationale: In stress incontinence, relaxed pelvic muscles and a weak urethra reduce urethral resistance, and anything that raises abdominal pressure pushes urine past the seal. Pregnancy, obesity, cystocele, and urethrocele add pressure or weaken support, and a smoker's chronic cough pounds the pelvic floor. An overactive detrusor is tempting because it also causes leaking, but it belongs to urge incontinence. Spinal cord injury causes reflex incontinence.
questions.takeaway: Stress incontinence comes from weak urethral resistance plus extra pressure: obesity, cough, pregnancy, cystocele, or urethrocele.
questions.hintContent: For each factor, decide whether it weakens the urethral seal or raises abdominal pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: When a SATA item names one type, include only factors that cause that type, not every cause of incontinence.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 80-year-old man with BPH constantly dribbles urine, and the nurse palpates a firm, distended bladder above the pubic bone. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Rely on absorbent pads as the main treatment
Perform a bladder scan to measure retained urine
Monitor for signs of a urinary tract infection
Notify the provider of the findings
Teach Kegel exercises as the main treatment
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pads manage the wetness but leave the full bladder untreated.
Correct. A bladder scan confirms how much urine is retained.
Correct. Stagnant urine in a bladder that does not empty grows bacteria, so UTIs are a clue and a risk.
Correct. The provider needs to know so the bladder can be drained and the cause treated, for example with catheterization, medication, or surgery.
Incorrect. Kegels strengthen the urethral seal for stress incontinence and do not relieve an obstruction.
questions.rationale: A wet client with a firm, distended bladder above the pubis has overflow incontinence from retention. The bladder will not empty, so the nurse assesses with a bladder scan and notifies the provider so the bladder can be drained and the obstruction treated, for example with medication, catheterization, or a TURP. Because urine sits stagnant, these clients are prone to UTIs. Pads are tempting because the client is wet, but mopping the floor does not fix the clog.
questions.takeaway: Overflow incontinence needs the bladder assessed and emptied, not just pads.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether the real problem is too much leaking or a bladder that will not empty.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA items, reject options that only manage the symptom when the cause is still untreated.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Managing Urinary Incontinence: Kegels, Bladder Training, Devices & Meds
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 46-year-old client with stress incontinence was taught Kegel exercises last week. She says, "I've been doing them by stopping my urine stream every time I go to the bathroom." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Good. Stopping the stream each time you void is the best way to do them."
"Try stopping the stream only during the first void of the morning instead."
"Hold the stream for a full minute each time to build the most strength."
"That's only for finding the muscles. Do the squeezes with an empty bladder."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Repeatedly stopping the stream can interfere with complete bladder emptying.
Incorrect. Doing the exercise while voiding at any time of day still risks incomplete emptying.
Incorrect. The hold is 3 to 10 seconds, and doing it while voiding is the problem.
Correct. Stopping the stream once helps the client find the right muscles, but the exercise itself is done with an empty bladder.
questions.rationale: Kegel exercises strengthen the pelvic floor and improve perineal muscle tone for both the bladder and the rectum. Clients find the muscles by noticing those used to stop the urine stream or resist a bowel movement. The exercise is then done with an empty bladder: tighten for 3 to 10 seconds, relax for 10 to 15 seconds, and repeat 10 times. Stopping the stream at each void is a common misunderstanding, and it can interfere with complete emptying.
questions.takeaway: Stopping the urine stream is only for finding the Kegel muscles; do the exercises with an empty bladder.
questions.hintContent: Separate how a client finds the muscles from how the exercise itself is done.
questions.hintStrategy: In teaching-correction items, choose the response that fixes the misconception and gives the right technique.

BPH smooth-muscle relaxer (first dose last night)
Dizzy on standing this morning; nearly fell in the bathroom; BP 92/54 mm Hg sitting
Unsure how often to apply the cream
